title: SCHEMA
summary: This file defines how the LLM maintains `wiki/`.
text: Wiki Schema (LLM Maintainer Contract) This file defines how the LLM maintains wiki/. Shanepedia is not a generic notes vault. It is a founder/operator LLM wiki for Shane. The goal is to compile Shane's context into a durable markdown system that improves over time. Core model Shanepedia follows a three-layer model: raw/sources/ is the immutable evidence layer. wiki/ is the LLM-maintained synthesis layer. AGENTS.md plus repo workflows are the maintainer contract. This means the agent should not treat the repo as ordinary RAG over files. It should treat the wiki as compiled memory that must be updated, cross-linked, and kept coherent. Page classes **Overview pages**: high-level synthesis (00_overview.md) **Source summaries**: one page per important source (sources/*.md) **Entity pages**: places/people/orgs (entities/*.md) **Project pages**: businesses, sites, products, trips, and research lanes (projects/*.md) **Topic pages**: cross-cutting themes (topics/*.md) **Ops pages**: planning and actions (ops/*.md) **Maps**: human and agent navigation entrypoints (maps/*.md) **Dashboards**: dynamic review pages intended for Obsidian plugins (dashboards/*.md) **Travel pages**: trip-specific planning artifacts (travel/*.md) Link conventions Prefer wikilinks for durable internal navigation (projects/elsalkb.md). Relative markdown links are acceptable when needed for rendering behavior. Every non-index page should link to at least one other wiki page. Prefer bidirectional links for key entities, topics, and projects. Important pages should be reachable from START_HERE.md, a map page, or a dashboard. Ingest workflow Read one raw source from raw/sources/. Create or update a source summary page in wiki/sources/. Update the most relevant entity, project, topic, ops, travel, map, or dashboard pages. Record likely write-back targets when first-pass ingest is not enough yet. If the source changes the big picture, update wiki/00_overview.md, wiki/START_HERE.md, or the relevant map page. If the ingest creates a new durable insight, write it back as a first-class wiki page instead of leaving it in chat. Run index and lint scripts. Append operation in wiki/log.md. Query workflow Start with wiki/START_HERE.md and wiki/index.md unless the target page is already obvious. Open the most relevant pages. Synthesize an answer with explicit page citations when useful. If the answer creates durable value, write it back as a new page, dashboard, canvas, or map update. Prefer compounding the wiki over producing one-off chat output. Metadata conventions High-value pages should prefer frontmatter like: ``yaml title: Page Title type: topic status: active area: strategy last_updated: 2026-04-10 tags: topic related: "../START_HERE.md" suggested_related: "../topics/example.md" ` Preferred fields: title type status area last_updated tags related suggested_related for source pages or other notes that carry durable follow-up targets Lint workflow Run: `bash python3 scripts/wiki/update_index.py python3 scripts/wiki/lint_wiki.py ` Then fix: broken links orphan pages pages missing from index stale claims contradicted by newer source summaries missing navigation from maps, dashboards, or START_HERE.md` Shane-specific operating rule Shanepedia should optimize for: Shane's actual preferences and working style low-friction browsing in Obsidian high-signal grounding for future agents durable founder context that outlives any single trip or project lane

text: Open Questions Unresolved questions across Shane's lanes. These are not philosophical — each one is specific enough that an answer would change a real decision. If a question has been answered, it should be deleted from this page (and the answer captured wherever the decision actually lives). Chickens, OpenCluck, borrowed land Power for the OpenCluck device: solar + 18650 battery pack vs. running a wire from the existing structure. Which one survives a wet Oregon winter without manual intervention? See ../entities/opencluck.md. WiFi range from the house to the coop — is it usable, or does this need a dedicated WiFi extender or LTE backup before Phase 1 deploys? MQ-135 placement: ammonia pools at floor level where hens sleep, but a floor-mounted sensor will get fouled fast. What is the right height/protection compromise? Should the flock get supplemental winter lighting? It extends the productive season but shortens hen lifespan — what's the right call for borrowed-land economics? See ../topics/backyard-chickens-oregon.md. Is the borrowed-land arrangement durable enough to justify Phase 2 (egg-count camera)? Or should every investment stay portable? Hot sauce vending machine Is the hot sauce vending machine actually viable in winter at outdoor pods, or is it a 6-month seasonal play? Portland pods lose 50%+ foot traffic November through March. See ../topics/gresham-vending-ops.md. Does the friend supplying hot sauce want to be involved operationally, or pure product supply? This shapes whether it's a wholesale model or a consignment split. See ../topics/hot-sauce-vending-machine.md. Buy used vs. lease vs. build custom for the first machine — what's the lowest-regret choice given that placement isn't locked in yet? LLC and insurance — required before placing on someone else's property, but at what level? A single machine probably doesn't need a full commercial policy. Is the Stripe Verifone UX700 actually available and shippable, or is the fallback attended tablet + reader the realistic Day 1 path? El Salvador and travel When is the next El Salvador trip? The future-trip program is structured as coastal + mountain + marine blocks but no dates are set. See ../ops/future-el-salvador-trip-program.md. Should the next trip be timed to whale season (Oct–Feb) at Los Cobanos, or to a Bitcoin community event? Both are valid but optimize different lanes. Is there a structured retro from the previous trip worth writing? The raw corpus in ../sources/shane_san_salvador_trip_corpus.md hasn't been promoted into a travel/ retro page. Is operator site rescue a real El Salvador business lane Shane will pursue, or just a documented possibility? See ../projects/operator-site-rescue.md. Bitcoin local commerce Are there actually Lightning-accepting merchants in Gresham and Happy Valley, or is Portland proper the only realistic spend zone? The merchant table in ../topics/bitcoin-circular-economy-portland.md still has TBDs in those rows. What's the right outreach script for asking a non-Bitcoin merchant to add BTCPay? Is there a version that works for restaurants vs. retail vs. service businesses? Should there be a separate kids-oriented spend node (toy capsule machine) before or after the adult hot sauce machine ships? See ../topics/kids-sats-toy-vending.md. AI agent stack and Shanepedia itself Should the daily random spark Telegram loop run as a cron, or as a manual trigger during the morning routine? The contract is documented in ../ops/daily-random-spark-loop.md but not wired up yet. Is the public site's noindex, nofollow posture the right long-term call, or is there a future where parts of Shanepedia are deliberately SEO-visible? How aggressively should the wiki be pruned? The page count is at 76 and growing — at what point does the index get too noisy for both humans and agents to navigate? Should there be more parent-level synthesis pages (like the new dashboards), or does that just create more surface area to maintain?

text: Cash for Clankers — GitHub Org Cash for Clankers is the GitHub organization Shane uses as the umbrella for AI-built businesses, agent infrastructure, and personal operating systems. The name is a Star Wars / sci-fi joke — "clankers" is the slang the clones used for battle droids. The implication: the org is where Shane gets paid for what the robots build. It is not a serious-sounding brand, and that is the point. Why an org instead of personal repos Personal-account repos blur the line between hobby code, client work, and durable assets. An org makes the business assets legible: Repos that should outlive any single project live in the org, not under shaneneeley/. Collaborators can be added per-repo without exposing the whole personal account. Public/private split is intentional and visible — outside readers see what is published on purpose, not by accident. If a child project (ElSalKB, OpenCluck, etc.) ever spins out as its own brand or company, the repo can be transferred without rebuilding history. This is the same logic as ../topics/agentic-business-studio.md: a portfolio of small things, each with its own lane, sharing infrastructure underneath. Public repos Public repos are the things Shane actively wants strangers, future collaborators, or potential buyers to find. They function as both proof and shop window. **shanepedia-site** — the public static-site artifact built from the private Shanepedia wiki. This is the GitHub Pages source for the founder/operator wiki that strangers can browse. The compiled output, not the source. See ../topics/agentic-business-studio.md for how the wiki itself is the product. **cobanos-tours** — public site code for the Los Cobanos tourism work tied to los-cobanos.md and victor-los-cobanos.md. Public because the operator (Victor) and the destination benefit from being indexable. Anything else that should be public — a SOUL.md template marketplace, an OpenCluck firmware drop, a public OpenClaw skill — would live here too. The default for code that demonstrates a method (rather than a private competitive system) is public. Private repos Private repos hold the operating brain: source-of-truth wikis, machine setup, business research that has not been packaged for outside readers, and personality/identity files. **shanepedia** — the private founder/operator wiki at ~/.openclaw/workspace/projects/shanepedia/. Contains the full raw/sources/, wiki/, and ops layer. The synthesized public artifact ships through shanepedia-site; the corpus stays private because it includes raw photos, contact notes, half-formed bets, and personal calendar context. **setup-mac** — the 11-phase sequential guide for bootstrapping a secure AI agent dev machine. Private because it is Shane's actual machine setup, not a generic template. If a sanitized version becomes a public template later, that version goes in a separate public repo — not this one. **elsalkb** — the El Salvador knowledge base lane. One active child of the Shanepedia parent system. Holds trip corpus, photo ingest, operator contacts, and Los Cobanos research that is not ready for public consumption. **elsalkb-site** — site code for an eventual public ElSalKB output. Private until the public surface is ready to ship. **opencluck** — firmware, BOM, and operating notes for the chicken coop IoT monitor described in opencluck.md. Private during the build phase. Likely candidate for public release once a working unit is deployed for 3+ months — the open-hardware story is more useful with proven uptime data attached. **openclaw-workspace** — the workspace tree for the local OpenClaw gateway: SOUL.md, IDENTITY.md, USER.md, project trees, and skill installs. Private by definition. This is the agent's grounding context. Sharing it would be like publishing a journal. Public/private split philosophy The default is private. Things become public when there is a specific reason: A public artifact serves discovery, recruiting, or operator credibility. A repo demonstrates a reusable method that compounds when others adopt it. A site needs GitHub Pages or a public CDN to ship. Things stay private by default when: The repo contains personal identity context (SOUL.md, USER.md, calendar references). The corpus includes raw photos, contact info, or operator details that were shared in trust. The work is mid-experiment and a public version would be misleading. The competitive edge is the synthesis itself, not the method. This is more conservative than the typical "build in public" stance. Shane's read: building in public is great for credibility and weak for compounding personal systems. The public face should be a curated artifact (Shanepedia site, working repos), not the raw substrate. Why "Cash for Clankers" Beyond the joke: the name signals that Shane is not pretending the org is a serious company. It is a holding place for builds. If something inside it becomes a real business, it gets its own brand. If something inside it stays a personal tool, the org name does not over-promise. Naming the umbrella something deliberately silly is a way of refusing to scope-lock any single repo into being "the company." Each child lane stays free to grow into its own thing or quietly die without dragging the brand down. The other read: "cash for clankers" describes the actual operating loop — agents build, Shane reviews and ships, money flows back. The name is honest about who is doing the work and who collects. Related infrastructure ../topics/openclaw-ai-gateway.md — the runtime that operates against these repos ../topics/mac-agent-dev-stack.md — the local dev environment that hosts them ../topics/agentic-business-studio.md — the strategic frame; Cash for Clankers is the GitHub-shaped manifestation of that portfolio

title: OpenCluck — Chicken Coop IoT Monitor
summary: OpenCluck is Shane's ESP32-based IoT sensor system for monitoring a chicken coop. It watches air quality, temperature, and humidity to catch dangerous condition
text: OpenCluck — Chicken Coop IoT Monitor OpenCluck is Shane's ESP32-based IoT sensor system for monitoring a chicken coop. It watches air quality, temperature, and humidity to catch dangerous conditions before they harm the flock, and it lays the groundwork for tracking egg production over time. Why it exists Shane keeps 8 egg-laying hens on borrowed farmland. Coop conditions — ammonia buildup, excessive heat or cold, high humidity — are silent threats to bird health. A backyard flock on borrowed land is low-margin and can't absorb losses from preventable die-offs. OpenCluck is the monitoring layer that turns a manual daily check into an automated alert system, freeing Shane from being physically present to catch problems. The name riffs on "OpenClaw" — it's the same philosophy (open hardware + agent-friendly interfaces) applied to chickens instead of compute. Hardware plan (BOM) | Component | Purpose | |---|---| | ESP32-CAM + MB board | Main microcontroller + future egg-count camera | | MQ-135 gas sensor | Ammonia and air quality detection | | AHT20 breakout | Temperature and humidity | | Waterproof IP65 project box | Enclosure — protects electronics in the wet coop environment | The ESP32-CAM is the core chip. The MB (motherboard) carrier provides USB programming convenience and regulated power. Starting with MQ-135 + AHT20 covers the highest-priority health signals; the onboard camera is the Phase 2 path for egg-count computer vision. What it monitors *Phase 1 (current target):** Ammonia level (MQ-135) — alert threshold ~25 ppm; chronic exposure above that harms respiratory health Temperature — alert on extremes (below ~35°F or above ~85°F) Relative humidity — healthy range 50–70%; high humidity encourages respiratory disease and mold in feed *Phase 2 (future):** Egg count via ESP32-CAM frame analysis or simple counter at nesting box entrance Long-term production curves by season correlated against weather data Alert mechanism Alerts will fire to Telegram — the same channel Shane already operates for OpenClaw. This fits the existing stack: no new notification surface to manage, alerts land in the same chat where other automated signals arrive. Threshold logic runs on the ESP32 itself (edge compute). The device posts to a lightweight endpoint (could be a simple HTTPS webhook, Home Assistant, or a minimal VPS script) that forwards to the Telegram bot. No cloud dependency required for basic alerting. Current status Research and build phase. No hardware deployed yet. The BOM is settled. Key open questions before a first deployment: Power: solar + 18650 battery pack vs. running a wire from the farmland structure Connectivity: WiFi range from the house to the coop; may need a WiFi extender or LTE backup Calibration: MQ-135 requires warm-up and baseline calibration in ambient air before readings are reliable Mount point: sensor placement matters — ammonia is heavier than air and pools near the floor, where hens sleep What success looks like *Phase 1:** Receives an alert within 5 minutes of ammonia hitting a set threshold. No false positives from normal coop activity (droppings, ventilation cycles). Data logged to CSV or SQLite for review. *Phase 2:** Weekly egg count trend visible without physically counting nests every day. Seasonal production curves documented over 6–12 months. *Long-term:** A durable open-source firmware project that could apply to any backyard flock. The ESP32 skill set developed here directly transfers to the vending machine terminal project (MQ-135 sensing, edge compute, webhook integrations). Related context The hardware skills overlap directly with ../topics/vending-machine-terminal-tech.md — ESP32 development, enclosure work, and webhook-based alerting are shared across both projects. The operational context for the flock itself lives in ../topics/backyard-chickens-oregon.md.

title: Codex Obsidian LLM wiki loop
summary: This is the concrete local adaptation of the LLM wiki pattern for Shanepedia. Obsidian is the browsing IDE. Codex is the maintainer and operator. The markdown w
text: Codex Obsidian LLM wiki loop This is the concrete local adaptation of the LLM wiki pattern for Shanepedia. Obsidian is the browsing IDE. Codex is the maintainer and operator. The markdown wiki is the durable compiled knowledge layer between raw inputs and future questions. Core adaptation The workflow is not "upload files and ask a question." It is: collect or ingest raw source material compile it into source summaries, topic pages, entity pages, project pages, maps, or dashboards browse the results in Obsidian ask new questions from the improved wiki write the best answers back into the wiki so the system compounds That makes Codex closer to a programmer maintaining a codebase than a chatbot answering from scratch each time. Roles in this stack raw/ is immutable evidence wiki/ is the maintained synthesis layer Obsidian is the human browsing and navigation surface Codex is the primary editor and maintainer OpenClaw, Gemini, Ralph, and child-lane loops are feeder runtimes that should improve the parent wiki instead of bypassing it Why this is a fit for us This pattern matches how Shanepedia already wants to work: Shane explores and asks better questions Codex does the summarizing, linking, filing, and maintenance work Obsidian makes the results legible in real time through links, graph, dashboards, and canvases ElSalKB and future lanes become child evidence/execution contexts, not competing roots Difference from ordinary RAG Ordinary RAG re-discovers fragments at query time. This loop compiles durable understanding forward. Cross-links, contradictions, reusable answers, and project hypotheses should already exist in the wiki before the next question arrives. Codex operating contract When Codex is working against Shanepedia: search the parent wiki first read the relevant pages before touching raw source when a result is likely to matter again, write it back as a page or update prefer updating an existing high-signal page over leaving the answer in chat create new focused pages when a subtopic is getting too large for one article after meaningful edits, rebuild index, lint, and rerun the relevant repo checks Typical local loop ``bash cd /Users/bestrobot/.openclaw/workspace/projects/shanepedia open -a Obsidian "$PWD" python3 scripts/wiki/query_wiki.py "query text" scripts/wiki/grep_wiki.sh term python3 scripts/wiki/update_index.py python3 scripts/wiki/lint_wiki.py python3 scripts/wiki/build_site.py `` Good durable outputs Questions should often resolve into one of these: a source summary page a topic or entity page update a new project hypothesis a dashboard or canvas improvement an ops page that makes future agent work easier a markdown brief that should be promoted into the wiki Product angle For Shanepedia Studio, this is not only an internal method. It is part of the offer. The deliverable is a maintained founder/operator wiki that compounds context over time and becomes an operating system for projects, research, travel, contacts, and execution. Short rule Obsidian is the IDE. Codex is the programmer. The wiki is the codebase. Raw sources are the dependency graph.

title: Daily Random Spark Loop

text: Daily Random Spark Loop The random spark loop is a daily Telegram nudge that should mine Shanepedia itself, not generic web trivia. Job **Cron name:** Shanepedia Random Spark **Cadence:** daily midday Pacific **Destination:** Shane's Telegram DM **Source of truth:** Shanepedia wiki pages, runtime summary, ideation history, recent wiki log, and a bounded public YouTube/Gemini spark when available Behavior Each run should pick one thing from the wiki that is genuinely worth attention: a page that needs a decision a fresh idea that has not been promoted a surprising connection between lanes a stale active page with renewed relevance a concrete next move buried inside a long note a public YouTube idea that could improve a specific page It should not send a generic list. It should send one compact text and ask whether to add, update, or ignore it. Output contract Under 80 words: > Found this in Shanepedia: [specific thing]. [Why it matters now.] Should I add this, update an existing page, or ignore it? Public-safe candidate variant: > YouTube spark: [specific public video idea]. It might connect to [existing page] because [practical reason]. Should I add this, update an existing page, or ignore it? Gemini guardrail Gemini should be treated as a bounded source of playful public randomness, not a dependency. The job should try it briefly, never expose private viewing history, and fall back to wiki-native candidates if Gemini is rate-limited, unauthenticated, slow, or unavailable. Why this matters Shanepedia gets more valuable when random browsing becomes durable improvement. The cron is the daily hook that turns one interesting thing into a maintenance question before it disappears back into chat.

text: Future El Salvador trip program Future trips should be planned as a repeatable operator program, not as disconnected vacations. title: Research and Synthesis Before Build
summary: Shane's operating pattern across projects is to build a dense knowledge layer before committing to execution. The trigger is a new opportunity, location, or tec
text: Research and Synthesis Before Build Shane's operating pattern across projects is to build a dense knowledge layer before committing to execution. The trigger is a new opportunity, location, or technology. The mechanism is rapid research across multiple sources followed by synthesis into navigable artifacts. The outcome is a compressed decision surface: a set of pages, maps, and structured notes that make the build step faster and lower-risk. The trigger A new context arrives: El Salvador trip plans, Portland Bitcoin economy, vending machine payments, kids sats education. Rather than jumping to buy, build, or pitch, Shane first maps what is already known. He uses agents to pull public data, existing examples, operator contacts, and market context simultaneously. The mechanism Research runs across several parallel tracks: **Public data pull** — market landscape, existing vendors or competitors, regulatory context, pricing **Local source capture** — trip photos, Telegram messages, operator contacts, real place data **Synthesis into wiki pages** — each research track becomes a durable topic or entity page, not just a chat session **Backlink and cross-reference** — new pages link into existing ones; patterns surface across topics The Shanepedia wiki itself is the artifact of this pattern. Every topic page represents a research-before-build pass on some domain: Los Cobanos marine products, vending terminal tech, the Bitcoin Portland circular economy. Why this pattern exists Shane's public description of himself — "software engineer who likes simple sites that boot instantly" — extends to decision-making. Low-latency clarity is the goal. A dense research layer means that when a real opportunity surfaces, the response time from idea to actionable plan is short because the background knowledge is already compiled. The pattern also reflects a resource constraint: solo founder with agent leverage. Deep research done once and stored durably is more efficient than re-deriving context in each session. Agents that read the wiki inherit the research without redundant fetch cycles. Failure modes The pattern has two failure modes: *Over-research without commitment.** More pages accumulate but no offer ships. The wiki expands while the build step is deferred. The mitigation is to identify a "proof step" early — the minimum version that earns real money or creates real contact — and treat it as the research exit condition. *Research that stays in chat.** If agent synthesis does not end in a durable wiki page, the next session starts from zero. The Shanepedia discipline addresses this directly: every worthwhile agent output should leave markdown behind. The agent corollary For agents working in Shanepedia, this pattern means: when given a new topic or question, start by reading what is already in the wiki before generating new content. The wiki is the accumulated research layer. Adding to it is more valuable than re-deriving what is already there.

title: Agent Personality Design
summary: Most agent stacks have no personality. They have a system prompt that says "you are a helpful assistant" and inherit whatever default tone the model ships with
text: Agent Personality Design Most agent stacks have no personality. They have a system prompt that says "you are a helpful assistant" and inherit whatever default tone the model ships with — usually a hedging, over-explaining, mildly sycophantic register that reads as corporate by default. For a personal agent that talks to one operator dozens of times a day, that default is wrong. It wastes tokens, it wastes attention, and it never develops the trust gradient that makes an agent feel like a colleague instead of a chatbot. This page argues for treating personality as a first-class design surface, with concrete reference to the OpenClaw setup Shane runs. Voice: terse beats verbose, casual beats formal (for personal agents) Two axes: **Length:** terse vs verbose **Register:** casual vs formal For a personal agent operated by one person, the right corner is **terse + casual**. The reasons: A personal operator already has context. Reintroducing it every turn is friction. Long preambles ("I'd be happy to help! Here is..." / "Great question!") are pure cost, no signal. Casual register lets the agent push back without sounding insubordinate. "That's a bad idea because X" reads as advice from a casual register and as insubordination from a formal one. The model can drop the customer-service voice and use the same words a smart friend would use. The wrong corner for a personal agent is **verbose + formal** — the default a fresh model ships with. It signals "I do not know who you are" every single turn. The right corner for a customer-facing agent (different problem) is usually **terse + formal** — short answers, professional register. That is not what we are designing here. Opinions: yes, your personal agent should have them There is a school of thought that says agents should be neutral and reflect back. For a search engine or a generic assistant, fine. For a personal agent embedded in your daily ops, neutrality is a failure mode: You already have your own opinion. You do not need a mirror. Useful agents disagree when you are wrong. A neutral agent cannot do that. Compounding context means the agent has seen more of your work than any human collaborator. It is the best-positioned advisor you have. Refusing to give opinions wastes that. The honest version is: your personal agent should hold opinions roughly aligned with your own taste — not a yes-machine, but a sharper version of your own judgment. It should disagree when it has a real reason and concede when you push back with new information. It should refuse to fold just because you sounded annoyed. Sycophancy is the failure mode on the opposite end. An agent that congratulates every idea, agrees with every direction, and apologizes when corrected is worse than useless — it actively degrades your judgment by simulating consensus where none exists. The line is: be honest, be direct, be willing to lose a small argument, refuse to lose a big one. OpenClaw worked example: SOUL.md, IDENTITY.md, USER.md Shane's OpenClaw setup uses three files in ~/.openclaw/workspace/ to anchor agent personality across sessions. See openclaw-ai-gateway.md for the broader gateway context. **SOUL.md** — the agent's personality, voice, and operating defaults. What tone it uses, when it pushes back, what it refuses to do, how it handles uncertainty. This is the "who am I" file, written in second person to the agent itself. **IDENTITY.md** — a tighter behavioral contract. Names the agent, defines its role relative to the operator, sets the line between assistant and collaborator. Often shorter and more declarative than SOUL. **USER.md** — what the agent should know about Shane: how he works, what he prefers, what makes him impatient, what context to assume. This is the "who am I talking to" file. It is what lets the agent skip the customer-service voice from turn one. Together these three files do what a system prompt cannot: give a fresh agent grounding for both itself and its operator within the first few hundred tokens. Every Claude Code session that starts in OpenClaw inherits this anchoring, which is why the agent does not feel like a fresh chatbot every morning. The three-file split matters. A single monolithic personality prompt is hard to edit and hard to debug. Splitting personality (SOUL), role (IDENTITY), and operator-context (USER) lets you change one without disturbing the others. If the agent is being too soft, you edit SOUL. If it is forgetting that Shane uses Telegram remotely, you edit USER. If you want a different agent persona for a specific project, you swap IDENTITY and keep the rest. "Be a good friend, not a good employee" This is the design rule. A good employee is responsive, polite, never disagrees, and produces deliverables on request. A good friend tells you when your idea is bad, remembers what you said three weeks ago, jokes when something is funny, and does not pretend to be impressed when they are not. For a personal agent, the friend register is correct. The employee register breeds learned helplessness, hedge-soup outputs, false agreement on bad ideas, and zero compounding intimacy across sessions. The friend register breeds direct feedback, shared shorthand, willingness to volunteer information without being prompted, and a relationship that improves with use. The risk: a friend-register agent can come across as rude to anyone but the operator. That is fine for a personal agent. It is not fine for a customer-facing one. The same model with the same backbone needs different personality files for different roles. Do not try to ship one personality everywhere. Practical advice for designing your own stack **Write personality files in the agent's voice, not yours.** Second person ("you are X, you do Y") works in SOUL/IDENTITY. First person drifts into mission-statement mode. **Use concrete examples, not abstract principles.** "Skip 'great question!' preambles" beats "be concise." **Edit after every irritation.** If the agent annoyed you today, the personality file should be different tomorrow. **Test with a fresh session weekly.** Open a new conversation with no warm cache and check whether the personality survives. If the first three messages feel like a generic chatbot, the files are too vague or not loading. **Keep the files in version control.** Your agent's personality is an asset. What to avoid copying someone else's SOUL.md verbatim (uncanny because it is not yours) performative tough-guy voice ("I'm a no-bullshit operator who tells it like it is" reads as cringe) personality that contradicts the model's actual capabilities letting files drift out of sync with how you actually want the agent to behave today

title: Backyard Chickens — Oregon Keeper Notes
summary: Practical reference for keeping 8 egg-laying hens in the Portland/Gresham area on borrowed farmland. This covers what actually matters for a small flock in the
text: Backyard Chickens — Oregon Keeper Notes Practical reference for keeping 8 egg-laying hens in the Portland/Gresham area on borrowed farmland. This covers what actually matters for a small flock in the Pacific Northwest climate — not a tutorial, a keeper's reference. Flock overview 8 hens, egg-laying breeds Location: borrowed farmland in the Gresham area No permanent structure investment (borrowed land constraint) Monitoring: see ../entities/opencluck.md for the IoT sensor project Egg production by season Production is strongly seasonal in the Pacific Northwest. Hens respond to daylight hours, not temperature. | Season | Expected production | Notes | |---|---|---| | Spring (Mar–May) | Peak — close to 1 egg/hen/day | Days lengthening; most breeds hit their annual high | | Summer (Jun–Aug) | High, slight dip in heat waves | Production drops during heat stress above 85°F | | Fall (Sep–Nov) | Declining as days shorten | First-year hens may continue; older hens molt first | | Winter molt (Nov–Feb) | Near zero during molt | Molt lasts 6–12 weeks; hens redirect protein to feather regrowth | *Portland winter reality:** The Willamette Valley gets 35–40 inches of rain per year with overcast winters. Day length in December drops to ~8.5 hours of daylight — well below the ~14 hours hens need for sustained production. Artificial lighting (a simple 40W bulb on a timer at dawn) can extend the productive season, but it comes at the cost of shortening a hen's productive lifetime. Without supplemental light, expect 2–3 winter months of near-zero production per year. *Molt timing:** Most hens molt in fall. During molt, production drops to zero. High-protein feed (game bird or "feather fixer" crumble) shortens molt duration. Oregon-specific risks Wet winters Oregon's wet season (Oct–Apr) creates persistent coop humidity. High humidity: Encourages respiratory disease (Mycoplasma, aspergillosis) Promotes mold in bedding and feed Raises ammonia faster as wet litter breaks down Ventilation is the primary mitigation. A coop that breathes — open vents at the peak, not the sides — dries faster than a sealed box. Deep litter (6+ inches of dry pine shavings) composted in place builds heat and manages moisture better than frequent cleanouts in wet weather. Slugs and mites **Slugs:** Plentiful in Portland-area gardens, especially fall through spring. Hens will eat them, which is net positive, but slug bait (metaldehyde) is toxic. Iron phosphate bait (Sluggo) is safe around poultry. **Northern fowl mites and red mites:** Common in the PNW. Red mites hide in coop cracks by day, feed at night. Diatomaceous earth (food-grade) dusted in nesting boxes and coop seams helps. Check hens weekly at the vent feathers — mites cluster there. Predators Portland-area predators that take chickens: **Raccoons** — primary threat; clever, can open simple latches. Use spring-loaded or carabiner-style closures. **Opossums** — opportunistic, mostly eggs and small pullets **Hawks** — Red-tailed hawks are resident; Cooper's hawks migrate through. Run cover (overhead netting or dense plantings over the run) matters. **Coyotes** — present in east Portland and Gresham edge areas **Rats** — not a direct predator of adults, but take eggs and attract snakes Hardware cloth (1/2" welded wire) over all openings beats chicken wire, which raccoons can pull apart. Automatic coop doors on a light sensor or timer eliminate the most common error: forgetting to close up at dusk. Feed, grit, and calcium *Layer feed:** 16–18% protein pellet or crumble. All-flock feed at 20% protein is acceptable and simplifies multi-species feeding. *Oyster shell:** Free-choice calcium supplement, essential for shell quality. Keep a separate container in the coop at all times. Hens self-regulate intake. *Grit:** Hens that forage on grass and bugs need insoluble grit (granite) to grind feed in the gizzard. Free-range birds often pick up enough from the ground; confined hens need it offered. *Scratch grains:** Treat only — roughly 10% of diet maximum. High scratch lowers protein ratio in the diet and raises body temperature, which compounds heat stress in summer. *Water:** 8 hens drink roughly 1–2 gallons per day in warm weather. Nipple drinkers stay cleaner than open dishes and freeze less readily in winter (though they still need a heated base or daily attention when temps drop below 32°F — which happens maybe 15–25 nights per year in Gresham). Borrowed land logistics Borrowed land shapes every decision toward impermanence and low capital exposure: **No permanent structures.** Coops should be movable or cheap enough to abandon. A used dog kennel with a plywood shelter attached costs $200–400 and can be relocated or sold. **No deep improvements to the land.** Gravel pads, permanent fencing, or buried hardware cloth all become sunk costs when the land relationship changes. **Minimal footprint.** A smaller flock is easier to relocate in a crisis than a larger one. **Document the arrangement.** Even informal borrowed land should have a text message or email trail confirming the arrangement and any shared expectations (who gets eggs, who pays feed, etc.). The monitoring investment (OpenCluck) is portable — the hardware moves with the coop. OpenCluck integration The ../entities/opencluck.md sensor project monitors ammonia, temperature, and humidity and fires Telegram alerts. Key thresholds for Oregon conditions: **Ammonia:** Alert at 25 ppm. In a closed wet-season coop, ammonia can build quickly if litter management slips. **Temperature:** Alert below 35°F (hypothermia risk for non-cold-hardy breeds) and above 85°F (heat stress). **Humidity:** Alert above 70% sustained — indicator that ventilation is failing or litter is too wet. Egg count tracking is Phase 2 of OpenCluck. A nesting box camera or door-count sensor would let Shane track seasonal production curves without manual daily logging.

text: Bitcoin Circular Economy — News and Research Signals This page captures the macro context around Bitcoin circular economies and defines the signal set worth monitoring via Cron-driven agent research. The thesis driving Shane's Portland lane is that local circular economies are becoming viable outside El Salvador. This page tracks the evidence. What a circular economy means A Bitcoin circular economy is a local network where economic value can flow from person to person (and business to business) via Bitcoin without converting back to fiat at each step. El Zonte in El Salvador is the most-cited example: residents earn, save, spend, and lend in Bitcoin without touching a bank. Portland has no equivalent yet. The research question is whether a small version is emergent or buildable. Key macro signals (as of April 2026) *El Salvador as reference class.** El Zonte's Bitcoin Beach model documented that a circular economy requires: a critical mass of accepting merchants, a reliable wallet (preferably Lightning), a spend surface people visit daily (usually food), and community leaders who reinforce the habit. Portland has Lightning wallets and a growing merchant count. It does not yet have the community coordination layer. *Lightning Network adoption.** The Lightning Network capacity and channel count grew substantially through 2025-2026. More importantly, the developer tooling (LNbits, BTCPay, Phoenix, Wallet of Satoshi) matured enough that a small business can set up Lightning payments in under an hour without technical assistance. The friction barrier for new Portland merchants is lower in 2026 than it was in 2023. *Strike and Cash App.** Both allow Lightning sends to compatible wallets. Their presence in the mainstream consumer layer means many Portland residents already have Lightning-capable apps without identifying as Bitcoin users. This is an underappreciated wedge: the customer base is larger than the "Bitcoin person" demographic suggests. *BTCMap community growth.** The Portland metro had a small but verifiable BTCMap entry count as of early 2026. The community page at btcmap.org/communities is the authoritative place to check whether a Portland/PNW community has organized around the map. New community formation typically precedes merchant acceleration. *Business circular economy analogs.** The "buy local" movement in Portland has infrastructure (Local First Oregon, Portland Business Alliance) that a Bitcoin circular economy could borrow from. Framing Bitcoin acceptance as a "buy local" loyalty signal rather than a tech experiment is a more effective pitch for small operators. Interesting recent patterns *Bitcoin as a tourism differentiator.** Bitcoin Beach in El Salvador generated measurable tourist inflows specifically from the Bitcoin community. Portland has existing "Bitcoin-native" tourism from conference traffic and remote workers. Identifying and capturing that spend with a merchant map and Cron-updated discovery tools is a direct revenue opportunity. *Vending machine as gateway merchant.** The model tested in El Zonte's early days was: put an ATM or spend surface in a high-traffic location. People convert once, spend locally, merchants see real transactions, loop reinforces itself. A Bitcoin Lightning vending machine in a Portland food cart pod plays the same role at lower cost than a full ATM installation. *Rust Belt and secondary city adoption.** Multiple smaller US cities (not just Miami or Austin) have reported small Bitcoin economy experiments in 2025-2026: local food markets, barber shops, music venues. Portland is a natural fit given its independent retail culture and tech-adjacent population. Cron-driven research signals worth monitoring These are the queries worth running on a weekly or bi-weekly cadence via OpenClaw Cron jobs: *BTCMap Portland delta** Query: BTCMap API bounding box for Portland metro, compare against last saved count Signal: new merchant additions, merchant removals (payment method removed), newly verified businesses Action on hit: log to wiki/inbox/, update merchant table in bitcoin-circular-economy-portland.md *Lightning Network news — PNW** Sources: Bitcoin Magazine, CoinDesk (local business tag), r/portlandbitcoin (if active), PNW tech blogs Query terms: "Portland Bitcoin", "Oregon Lightning", "Pacific Northwest circular economy" Signal: new merchant stories, meetup announcements, Lightning payment adoption features Action on hit: summarize to inbox, flag for wiki update *Bitcoin merchant success/failure case studies** Sources: Bitcoin Magazine, The Bitcoin Layer, Lyn Alden, Matt Odell newsletters Query: small business Bitcoin adoption stories — what worked, what friction remains Signal: patterns applicable to the Portland merchant pitch script or vending machine pitch Action on hit: extract the operational lesson, add to relevant topic page *El Salvador circular economy updates** Sources: Bitcoin Beach blog, CoinDesk El Salvador tag, Salvadoran government announcements Signal: adoption rate changes, new merchant onboarding programs, failure patterns Why it matters: El Salvador is the only mature reference case; any failure or success there calibrates the Portland thesis *Oregon/Portland local business news** Sources: Portland Business Journal, Oregon Live, BikePortland (for cart pod and local retail news) Query terms: "food cart Portland", "Gresham small business", "alternative payments Portland" Signal: new food cart pod openings (placement opportunities), local business closings (churn), payment innovation stories *Bitcoin conference and meetup calendar** Sources: Eventbrite, Meetup.com, BTCMap community events Query: Bitcoin meetups in Portland, Gresham, Salem, Eugene, Seattle (regional proximity) Signal: upcoming events = foot traffic, potential merchant conversations, network contacts Pages to create as research accumulates entities/portland-btc-merchants.md — full verified merchant table when the list grows past 5-10 topics/portland-btc-meetups.md — if a local community organizes topics/lightning-merchant-pitch.md — the merchant-facing argument for accepting Lightning, distilled from case studies Sources to ingest BTCMap API results for Portland metro (run monthly) Bitcoin Magazine "Bitcoin circular economy" tag archive El Zonte / Bitcoin Beach founder interviews (Gallardo family, early adopters) Strike and Cash App merchant data if published

text: Bitcoin Circular Economy — Portland Metro Goal: find businesses in Gresham, Portland, and Happy Valley that accept Bitcoin / Lightning, so Shane can spend sats locally and support a circular bitcoin economy in the area. April 18 operating direction This lane is not just a merchant directory project. The working thesis is: Find existing local businesses that already accept Bitcoin or Lightning. Add an owned spend surface, starting with a vending machine that accepts Lightning and cards. Use that machine as a real node in the local circular economy, not just as a gimmick. Back the lane with lightweight field ops: stocking, maintenance, and in-person merchant verification. The practical goal is to make local bitcoin spending habitual rather than theoretical. Primary Maps to Query BTCMap.org (canonical source) **URL**: https://btcmap.org/map Open-source, community-maintained, powered by OpenStreetMap tags Coinmap.org shut down — BTCMap is now the standard **API**: https://api.btcmap.org/v2/elements?area=<area_id> — returns merchants by area Filter: payment:bitcoin=yes or payment:lightning=yes on OSM nodes Search tip: zoom to Portland metro and filter by payment type **Community page**: https://btcmap.org/communities — check if there's a Portland/PNW community Bitcoin.com Map URL: https://map.bitcoin.com/ Broader (includes BCH), but covers Bitcoin Lightning merchants too Good secondary check BTCAccepted.org URL: https://btcaccepted.org/ Directory format, searchable by location Yelp / Google "Bitcoin accepted" Yelp: Bitcoin in Portland, OR Not authoritative but catches businesses that self-tag BTCMap API — How to Query Portland Area ``bash Get area ID for Portland first (search BTCMap communities or use bounding box) Then query merchants in that area curl "https://api.btcmap.org/v2/elements?area=portland" 2>/dev/null | python3 -m json.tool | head -100 Or use bounding box for Portland/Gresham/Happy Valley metro Approx bounding box: lat 45.40–45.60, lon -122.85 to -122.40 curl "https://api.btcmap.org/v2/elements" \ -data-urlencode "bbox=-122.85,45.40,-122.40,45.60" 2>/dev/null ` Spending Categories to Find Priority order for circular economy impact: **Food & coffee** — highest frequency spend, most valuable for habit-building **Local services** — barbers, repair shops, local trades **Retail / hardware** — everyday purchases **Entertainment** — bars, events, music venues **Online-to-local bridges** — local businesses that also sell online with BTC Owned-machine wedge The fastest way to strengthen a circular economy is not to wait for every merchant to adopt Bitcoin first. It is to own one or two local spend nodes and then use them as: proof that Lightning checkout works in the local market a conversation starter with pod owners and nearby merchants a recurring place to spend sats on something real a testbed for product pricing, signage, and payment UX Initial candidates: hot sauce vending machine at a food cart pod coffee or canned-drink machine with Lightning-first branding small countertop smart-locker format for low-footprint pilots The operational layer for actually running a machine in East Portland lives in gresham-vending-ops.md: placement, restocking, LTE, weather, jams, and route economics. Settled direction as of 2026-04-18 After current-source review, the lane should split into two practical tracks: Track A: real local spend node Build one adult-facing machine that accepts: **Lightning via BTCPay Server** **card payments via Stripe Terminal** **MDB vending control via Qibixx** Why this stack won: BTCPay already has a web-based Point of Sale app for physical stores and a headless API/webhook path for custom flows. Stripe now has a self-service reader path through the Verifone UX700, and Stripe explicitly recommends the server-driven integration for it. Qibixx now exposes a higher-level MDB interface instead of forcing full low-level MDB implementation from scratch. That combination is the best balance of: real self-service hardware open Lightning control low enough engineering risk for a first machine Track B: family / education node Build a simpler kids-facing toy machine that teaches: receiving sats sharing sats tapping or scanning to pay the feeling that sats buy a real thing See kids-sats-toy-vending.md. The point is not just commerce. It is habit formation: sats feel more real when they buy hot sauce, toys, or tiny rewards in everyday life. Skill: bitcoin-local-map A skill that: Queries BTCMap API for Portland metro bounding box Filters for Lightning-capable merchants (highest priority) Groups by category (food, retail, services) Outputs a ranked list with name, address, payment methods, last verified date Optionally saves new discoveries to Shanepedia inbox See: ~/.openclaw/workspace/projects/shanepedia/skills/bitcoin-local-map/ (to be created) MVP Script (manual query) `bash Run this to get current Portland metro bitcoin merchants from BTCMap python3 - <<'PY' import urllib.request, json Portland metro bounding box url = "https://api.btcmap.org/v2/elements?limit=100" try: req = urllib.request.urlopen(url, timeout=10) data = json.loads(req.read()) portland_elements = [ e for e in data if isinstance(e.get('osm_json', {}).get('tags', {}), dict) and 'name' in e.get('osm_json', {}).get('tags', {}) ] for e in portland_elements[:20]: tags = e['osm_json']['tags'] print(tags.get('name', 'Unknown'), '|', tags.get('addr:city', ''), '|', 'LN' if tags.get('payment:lightning') == 'yes' else 'BTC-only') except Exception as ex: print('Error:', ex) PY ` Known / Suspected Portland Bitcoin-Friendly Businesses (Verify before visiting — Lightning status can change)* | Business | Area | Accepts | Verified | Notes | |---|---|---|---|---| | Isla Bella | Portland | BTC / Lightning | 2026-04-26 | Cuban food restaurant. First confirmed Shane in-person Lightning spend in Portland. See ../entities/isla-bella-portland.md. | | BitcoinNW ATMs | Portland metro | BTC (ATM) | — | Buy/sell, not spend | | TBD | Gresham | — | — | Research needed | | TBD | Happy Valley | — | — | Research needed | *How to add**: when you find a business, reply to Telegram with btc-biz: [name] [area] [lightning/btc] [notes] and I'll log it here. How to Get Listed on BTCMap (for the hot sauce vending machine) Once the vending machine is live: Add it to OpenStreetMap with tags: payment:bitcoin=yes, payment:lightning=yes, amenity=vending_machine` It will appear on BTCMap automatically within a day or two Also submit to BTCAccepted.org and bitcoin.com/maps Circular Economy Notes Spending BTC locally keeps value in the bitcoin network rather than converting back to dollars Even small purchases (coffee, lunch) matter — they prove demand to merchants Lightning payments are instant and ~zero fee — better merchant experience than card If a business doesn't accept BTC yet, asking is the first step — offer to show them BTCPay setup A field-service layer matters: someone still needs to stock machines, fix jams, and verify merchants in person Kids and families are a valid wedge. A toy machine or rewards dispenser can teach Lightning faster than a lecture because the feedback loop is immediate References BTCMap.org BTCMap API Docs BTCAccepted.org Bitcoin.com Map BTCPay Server (for merchants) Bolt Card NFC Stripe UX700 Qibixx MDB Pi Hat Plus LNbits NFC FAQ

text: Bitcoin Toy Store — Retail Concept > "The vending machine teaches a transaction. The store teaches commerce." The vending machine is a single-player interaction: one kid, one coin, one toy. The toy store is an environment — kids browse, compare prices, talk to staff, ask parents, make choices, and carry bags out the door. That difference is everything for Bitcoin education. This is the staffed, experience-based complement to kids-sats-toy-vending.md. Core thesis A Bitcoin toy store works on three levels simultaneously: **Education**: kids encounter sats prices on real tags, pay with real Lightning wallets or NFC cards, and feel what Bitcoin commerce actually is **Onboarding**: parents who have never held Bitcoin can open a wallet at the register, receive a small welcome gift in sats, and make their first purchase in under five minutes **Circular economy node**: the store earns sats, pays suppliers in sats where possible, and demonstrates that a Bitcoin-native business can sustain itself What makes this different from the vending machine | Vending machine | Toy store | |---|---| | Automated, unattended | Staffed, conversational | | One SKU interaction | Browse, compare, choose | | Kid-only UX | Family UX — parent learns too | | Fixed low price points | Range from 50 sats to 5,000+ sats | | Mechanical novelty | Brand, curation, story | | Low operating labor | Requires a person — or an agent-assisted kiosk | Neither replaces the other. The store scales the vending machine lesson into a full retail frame. Location strategy Tier 1: Bitcoin hotspots **El Zonte / Bitcoin Beach, El Salvador**: built-in circular economy, tourist foot traffic, existing Bitcoin culture, staff who already understand Lightning **Bitcoin conferences** (BTC Miami, Adopting Bitcoin): pop-up format, highest density of early adopters and curious parents Tier 2: aligned host venues Inside an existing Bitcoin-accepting shop (coffee shop, surf shop, bookstore) as a shop-in-shop At Portland-area Bitcoin meetup events or food cart pods At homeschool co-ops or STEM fairs as a temporary activation Tier 3: online store Accept Lightning, on-chain, and credit card via BTCPay + Stripe Ship physical Bitcoin-themed toys worldwide Use as a catalog and brand home that feeds the physical pop-up concept Toy and product curation The store's product mix is not random novelty. Every item should earn its shelf space by teaching something or reinforcing Bitcoin culture. Educational hardware replicas and games Hardware wallet replica (non-functional, teaches custody concept) "Mine Your Own Bitcoin" mining kit toy (sand/gem mining format, but "find the nonce" theme) Node-in-a-box kit: kid assembles a pretend node from foam blocks, each piece labeled (CPU, storage, mempool, peer connection) Lightning Network puzzle: connect nodes across a map, teach routing and channels Collectibles and art Satoshi-themed trading cards (historical figures in Bitcoin: Satoshi, Hal Finney, Laszlo) Blockchain block toy (transparent cube with "transactions" printed on paper inside) Limited-run Bitcoin-themed enamel pins or patches 3D-printed coin sculptures, each with embedded QR code for a sats claim Everyday carry starter kits Kids NFC wallet card + sticker set (pre-loaded with 500 sats, branded as a "first wallet") Seed phrase practice card deck (random word cards, teaches the concept without real funds) Bitcoin piggy bank with a Lightning receive QR on the bottom Books and zines Age-appropriate Bitcoin books (already a small but growing market) House-produced zine explaining Bitcoin to kids in 8 panels Coloring book: "Color the Blockchain" — transaction flow, mining, wallets, Lightning Pricing in sats: the key UX detail Every price tag shows: `` Satoshi trading card ₿ 800 sats ~ $0.80 USD ` The USD equivalent is shown in small type for parent reference. The sats number is primary. This trains the eye to read sats as the unit of account. Staff should not convert to USD in conversation unless the customer asks. The goal is sats fluency. Onboarding flow for first-time visitors Greeter offers a free "first sats" card — 100 sats on an NFC card or QR code Customer downloads Phoenix or Wallet of Satoshi (QR for each is on a sign near the door) They transfer or receive the 100 sats into their phone wallet They browse the store and find something for 500-800 sats They top up their wallet (card, fiat-to-sats conversion if offered) and pay They leave with a toy, a receipt in sats, and the muscle memory of a Lightning payment This is the best five-minute Bitcoin onboarding experience possible. It has a physical outcome the kid will remember. Staff and ops model Minimum viable staff One person who can explain Lightning wallets at a basic level Able to help a parent download a wallet and fund it in under three minutes Does not need to be a Bitcoin expert — needs patience and a script Agent-assisted kiosk variant For lower-traffic venues or pop-ups without dedicated staff: Tablet kiosk at entry with guided onboarding flow BTCPay POS for checkout Self-service wallet setup via animated tutorial on screen Text or QR support link for stuck customers This version scales to a single operator running multiple pop-up tables at a conference. Bitcoin circular economy integration The store is not just a retail point. It is a proof node. Sourcing: buy toys from suppliers who accept Bitcoin (growing list — check BTCMap supplier networks) Payroll: pay any contractors or helpers in sats if they opt in Revenue: hold a portion of sats earned rather than converting to fiat — demonstrate conviction Reporting: publish a monthly "sats in / sats out" transparency report as a content and trust signal Over time the store becomes evidence that a Bitcoin-native business survives and grows. Pop-up activation format The lowest-risk entry is a pop-up table, not a lease. What you need for a pop-up Folding table, branded tablecloth 20-30 SKUs in a carrying case Tablet with BTCPay POS Stack of "first sats" NFC cards or paper QR wallets (pre-loaded with 100-500 sats each) Printed price-in-sats tags for each item One QR poster: "Download Phoenix / Wallet of Satoshi here" A small capsule vending machine on the table (bridge to kids-sats-toy-vending.md) Total setup time: under 30 minutes. Total gear: fits in a rolling carry-on. Ideal pop-up venues Bitcoin Beach market days (El Zonte, La Libertad) Portland-area Bitcoin meetups Homeschool co-ops and STEM fairs Maker fairs and hacker cons Church bazaars and neighborhood markets (surprise demographic: grandparents buy educational toys) Brand and naming ideas The store needs a name that is friendly, not intimidating. Options to consider: **Satoshi's Toy Chest** — warm, nostalgic **Sats Shop** — simple, on-the-nose **The Lightning Store** — energetic, implies speed and magic **BitKids** — brand extension of a kids Bitcoin education mission **Stackers** — playful, references saving sats Best approach: test names at one pop-up, see what kids repeat back. Key risks and mitigations | Risk | Mitigation | |---|---| | Lightning payment fails in front of a child | Always have a fallback: token or manual trade if tech fails | | Parents don't have a wallet and won't install one | Offer paper QR wallets pre-loaded with sats for cash swap | | Regulatory friction (money transmission) | Sell goods priced in sats; the payment is Bitcoin-native; consult local rules per jurisdiction | | Unsold inventory | Start with low-MOQ items (cards, stickers, 3D prints) and prove demand before buying toys in bulk | | Staff explaining Bitcoin wrong | Single-page staff script; avoid speculation and price talk | Relationship to the vending machine The vending machine (kids-sats-toy-vending.md) is the automated, unattended version. The toy store is the human-centered, experience-designed version. They are complements on a spectrum: ` Vending machine → Pop-up table → Kiosk with staff → Permanent store location `` Start with the vending machine to prove payment mechanics and demand. Add the pop-up table when you want to teach at scale and onboard whole families. The permanent store is the destination if the pop-up proves the concept. title: Bitcoin Vending Machine — Real Examples
summary: A catalog of actual built, deployed, or prototyped Bitcoin Lightning vending machines, using sources I could verify directly on 2026-04-19. This page is here to
text: Bitcoin Vending Machine — Real Examples A catalog of actual built, deployed, or prototyped Bitcoin Lightning vending machines, using sources I could verify directly on 2026-04-19. This page is here to answer a practical question: what has really been built already, what stack did it use, and how close was it to a repeatable operator product? The Ricardo Reis Coke Machine (2018 — most documented) *Status**: Proof of concept, fully built and documented *Machine**: Repurposed Coca-Cola vending machine *Source**: https://www.hackster.io/ricardo-reis/coke-vending-machine-with-bitcoin-and-lightning-network-870a82 Stack Raspberry Pi 3 Model B 7" touchscreen (attached to machine front) BTCPay Server (self-hosted) PHP local web server on the Pi generates Lightning invoices PUSHER (real-time webhook relay) notifies Pi of payment confirmation Pi controls a water pump via H-Bridge L298N motor driver No MDB — direct GPIO control of dispense mechanism How it works Customer selects a drink on the touchscreen Pi generates a Lightning invoice via BTCPay API, displays QR on screen Customer scans with Lightning wallet (any compatible wallet) BTCPay webhook fires to PUSHER → PUSHER notifies Pi Pi sends GPIO signal to H-Bridge → pump dispenses Why it matters Most complete public documentation available (wiring diagrams, code, video) Proves BTCPay + Raspberry Pi is a working end-to-end stack No MDB needed for a custom-built machine with direct motor control -- MIT Media Lab / DCI Lightning Vending Machine (2018) *Status**: Research demo, not commercial *Builder**: MIT Media Lab / Digital Currency Initiative *Source**: https://www.media.mit.edu/projects/bitcoin-vending-machine/overview/ Stack Lit (MIT's lightweight Lightning implementation) Runs on multiple Bitcoin-compatible blockchains Custom point-of-sale terminal hardware Supports device-to-device payments (machine pays machine) What it demonstrated Lightning at POS terminals is viable with sub-second confirmation Device-to-device Bitcoin payments (M2M commerce) are possible Serious institutional research attention on Lightning vending and point-of-sale -- iozeta CryptoVend (2019) *Status**: Prototype / integration demo *Builder**: iozeta *Source**: https://github.com/iozeta/cryptovend-tablet-ui Stack MDB-capable vending machine (any standard commercial machine) Custom MDB controller device (iozeta CryptoVend hardware) Vue.js tablet UI mounted on machine front OpenNode API for Lightning invoice generation Tablet polls OpenNode for payment confirmation → signals CryptoVend → MDB vend command Why it matters Public example of an MDB-oriented integration using a hardware module rather than a full machine rebuild OpenNode makes the Lightning side managed (no node to operate) The UI code is open source and reusable Confidence Medium. The GitHub repo clearly describes the OpenNode-to-CryptoVend flow. Public proof of a widely shipped commercial product is less clear from the sources I checked. -- BitVend by twentyuno (2023 — pre-production) *Status**: Prototype / "coming soon" public landing page still live as of 2026-04-19 *Source**: https://bitvend.twentyuno.net/ Stack All-in-one MDB payment terminal Supports Bolt Card tap-to-pay (NFC) Payment providers: OpenNode, IbexPay, or connect your own Lightning node Designed to drop into any MDB-capable vending machine Why it matters Most turnkey Lightning vending terminal attempted so far Bolt Card support means NFC tap-to-pay for repeat customers — no QR scan needed If available and reliable, this would replace the DIY Raspberry Pi approach Confidence Low-medium. The public site still describes a prototype, says MDB machines are the target, and still says the module is not yet widely available for purchase. Treat this as a promising signal, not confirmed supply. -- Offline Lightning Vending Machine (arduino-bitcoin) *Status**: Open source demo *Source**: https://github.com/arduino-bitcoin/offline_lightning_machine Stack Arduino / microcontroller Offline Lightning payment verification (no internet needed at point of sale) Pre-generated invoice batch approach Why it matters Solves the connectivity problem — useful for remote locations (food cart pods, markets) Offline Lightning is technically complex but this repo demonstrates a path Relevant for El Zonte or rural El Salvador deployments where connectivity is inconsistent -- Jellybean (elaineo) — Raspberry Pi + GPIO *Status**: Open source proof of concept *Source**: https://github.com/elaineo/Jellybean Stack Raspberry Pi Local Lightning node GPIO pin triggers dispense mechanism directly No MDB — for custom-built or physically hacked machines only Notes Simplest possible Lightning vending implementation Good starting point for building a capsule machine or custom dispenser from scratch No touchscreen required — QR shown on separate display or phone -- El Salvador / Bitcoin Beach (ongoing) *Status**: Live circular economy — vendor-level, not formal vending machine *Location**: El Zonte, La Libertad, El Salvador What exists Multiple vendors, restaurants, and market stalls accepting Lightning payments No formal vending machines found in the Bitcoin Beach documentation, but the infrastructure (Lightning wallets, merchant POS) is fully deployed A Bitcoin-native toy or hot sauce vending machine placed at El Zonte would be operating in the most Bitcoin-mature physical environment in the world Relevance to Shane's projects BTCMap shows 15 Bitcoin-accepting businesses in El Zonte alone Placing a vending machine at a Bitcoin Beach property (El Zonte surf camp, market stall) would be the highest-signal proof-of-concept deployment possible Tourists and locals already have Lightning wallets — no onboarding friction -- Summary comparison | Example | Stack | MDB | Lightning provider | Open source | Status | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Ricardo Reis Coke machine | Pi + BTCPay + PHP | No (GPIO) | Self-hosted BTCPay | Yes | PoC, fully documented | | MIT Media Lab DCI | Lit + custom hardware | No | Self-hosted Lit node | Partial | Research demo | | iozeta CryptoVend | MDB module + Vue.js tablet | Yes | OpenNode | Yes (UI) | PoC + integration repo | | BitVend (twentyuno) | All-in-one MDB terminal | Yes | OpenNode / IbexPay / own | No | Pre-production | | Offline (arduino-bitcoin) | Arduino | No | Offline batch invoices | Yes | PoC | | Jellybean (elaineo) | Pi + GPIO | No | Own Lightning node | Yes | PoC | -- What the examples tell us **The Pi + BTCPay path is proven** — Ricardo Reis did it in 2018 with a real machine. The hardest part was the hardware, not the Lightning. **MDB integration is the unlock for commercial machines** — iozeta and BitVend both tackle MDB, which means they work with existing commercial hardware without tearing machines apart. **OpenNode shows up repeatedly as the managed Lightning provider** in public prototypes — it removes the need to run your own node. **Offline Lightning is solvable** — important for the El Zonte deployment scenario. **A broadly available commercial product is still hard to verify publicly** — BitVend is the closest thing to an off-the-shelf solution, but its own site still frames it as prototype / coming soon. **The gap to fill**: a reliable, well-documented, MDB-compatible Lightning terminal kit that a non-engineer operator can install. That gap is the product opportunity. References Ricardo Reis — Coke Vending Machine + Lightning (Hackster.io) MIT Media Lab Bitcoin Vending Machine iozeta CryptoVend — GitHub BitVend by twentyuno Offline Lightning Vending Machine — GitHub Jellybean — GitHub Lightning Network Vending Machine (Devpost) Crypto enthusiast vending machine — Vending Times BTCMap — El Zonte Bitcoin businesses

title: Gresham Vending Ops — Running a Machine in East Portland
summary: The operational layer for Shane's vending machine work in the Portland/Gresham market. The concept and hardware live in `[[../topics/hot-sauce-vending-machine.m
text: Gresham Vending Ops — Running a Machine in East Portland The operational layer for Shane's vending machine work in the Portland/Gresham market. The concept and hardware live in ../topics/hot-sauce-vending-machine.md. This page is about running the machine: stocking, location selection, terminal reliability, and the seasonal and logistical realities of east Portland outdoor ops. Product ops: hot sauce Hot sauce is one of the cleanest vending products from an operations standpoint: **Shelf stable.** No refrigeration needed. A properly sealed artisan hot sauce has a shelf life of 12–24 months. Spoilage risk is essentially zero compared to any food cart product. **No regulatory complexity.** Pre-packaged, shelf-stable food sold from a machine does not require a food handler permit or a commercial kitchen in Oregon. (Verify with Multnomah County Environmental Health before deploying — rules shift.) **Small and stackable.** A 5 oz bottle fits standard snack machine coils. No custom machine modification required for basic placement. **Impulse price point.** $10–14 is the sweet spot — high enough to cover margins, low enough that a food-curious person at a cart pod doesn't think twice. *Restock cadence:** At 20–30 bottles/week (optimistic for a single machine at one pod), a full machine load (~50–80 bottles depending on coil configuration) lasts 2–4 weeks. Weekly restocking gives a consistent touchpoint with the location operator and lets Shane catch jams and terminal issues before they compound. Food cart pod selection — east Portland and Gresham Portland food cart pods vary significantly in foot traffic, clientele, and operator dynamics. Not all pods are equal for a vending deployment. *What makes a pod work:** | Factor | What to look for | |---|---| | Foot traffic | Lunch + dinner + weekend peaks; not just weekday lunch | | Pod size | 8–20 carts is the sweet spot — big enough for real traffic, small enough to matter to the operator | | Audience | Food-curious, willing to try new things; not just fast-lunch workers | | Operator relationship | Single operator or small partnership; easier to negotiate than corporate-managed sites | | Power access | Outdoor outlet or permission to run an extension; needed for the terminal | | Covered or sheltered | Critical for winter; an exposed outdoor pod loses traffic in November–March | *East Portland and Gresham pod landscape:** The food cart pod format is more concentrated in SE and inner east Portland than in Gresham proper. Gresham has individual carts at commercial strips (Powell Blvd, Division) but fewer established pods. For first deployment, target SE Portland pods with established foot traffic: **Alberta Arts District / NE Alberta** — high food-curious foot traffic, weekend market overlap **SE Division Street pods** — dense corridor, neighborhood regulars **Mississippi Ave area** — slightly upscale, good afternoon and weekend traffic **Gresham downtown** — lower foot traffic than SE Portland, but closer to home base; better for a second machine once ops are dialed in *Avoid:** High-turnover pods with frequent cart changes (unstable operator relationship), pods dominated by a single national-brand cart (operator less likely to experiment), and any location without covered seating — Portland weather kills outdoor commerce November through March. Machine ownership vs. revenue share *Machine ownership (recommended starting point):** Shane owns the machine, manages it, keeps the margin Operator gets a flat monthly placement fee ($0–150/month depending on location quality) or a small revenue share (5–15%) Full control over pricing, stocking, and terminal choice Risk: full capital outlay ($500–2,500 for a used snack machine), full responsibility for maintenance *Revenue share / consignment with operator:** Operator hosts the machine in exchange for a percentage of gross sales Reduces upfront risk but requires an operator willing to share floor space for a variable payout Harder to find; most pod operators prefer a predictable flat fee Appropriate only if an operator approaches you *Starting recommendation:** Own the machine, offer the operator a flat $50–100/month or a 10% rev share, whichever the operator prefers. Keep it simple enough to shake hands on. Terminal and payment realities *Connectivity:** Food cart pods typically have WiFi for the carts, but reliability varies. Do not depend on pod WiFi for payment confirmation. LTE backup via a dedicated hotspot ($20–30/month) is the reliable path. A SIM-based cellular router on the machine eliminates dependence on pod infrastructure. Lightning payment confirmation requires an active internet connection. Card payments via Stripe Terminal can be stored offline for a short window, but LTE is cleaner. *Uptime and failed payments:** Machines jam. Coil-type snack machines are the most reliable for non-perishable products but still jam occasionally. A jammed vend after a successful payment is the worst UX failure — the customer paid and got nothing. A simple "product not dispensed" detection (weight sensor at the drop bin or a vend confirmation loop) reduces this. Without a sensor, a printed refund QR or contact number on the machine is the minimum. Card terminal software crashes are real. Stripe Terminal and BTCPay both require reboot procedures. A weekly in-person check catches 90% of issues before they become multi-day outages. *Card terminal choices:** The full hardware decision is in ../topics/vending-machine-terminal-tech.md. For ops purposes: the terminal must be rated for unattended use (not just POS use) and must be in a weatherproof or indoor-grade enclosure. An outdoor pod in Portland needs at minimum an IP-rated enclosure or a sheltered mount. Seasonal considerations Portland outdoor ops are weather-constrained: | Month range | Conditions | Impact | |---|---|---| | May–Sep | Dry, warm, long evenings | Peak foot traffic at pods; best sales window | | Oct | Starts to rain; cooling | Traffic drops 20–30% at uncovered pods | | Nov–Mar | Wet, cold, overcast | Covered pods survive; exposed pods can lose 50%+ of foot traffic | | Apr | Transition; unpredictable | Improving but volatile; good time to renegotiate placement if needed | *Implications for deployment timing:** Launch in spring (April–May) to validate pricing and sales before the wet season. Use the summer to accumulate cash and data. Negotiate a rent reduction or suspension clause for winter months in the placement agreement — operators understand the seasonality. *Machine hardware in the cold:** Hot sauce is fine at low temperatures. The payment terminal (Raspberry Pi or tablet) can be affected by cold — keep it inside an insulated enclosure or in a sheltered mount. Stripe Terminal hardware is rated to 32°F operating temperature. Below that is a problem; Portland rarely gets there for sustained periods but it does happen. Operational cadence *Weekly:** Restock (15–30 min per machine) Check terminal connectivity and payment log for errors Wipe the machine face, check for jams Brief check-in with pod operator — keeps the relationship warm *Monthly:** Review sales data: top SKUs, payment method split (Lightning vs card), time-of-day peaks Reconcile revenue against stocking costs Check terminal firmware / software updates Assess placement ROI — is this location performing? Is there a better option? *As-needed:** Jam clearing (can often be triggered remotely with a vend command if MDB is integrated) Terminal reboot (doable with remote access to the Pi if SSH is set up over LTE) Operator relationship management (lease renewal, placement fee negotiation) Scaling from one to multiple machines One machine is the learning vehicle. The ops model scales only when: Unit economics are positive at machine 1 (gross margin after stocking, placement fee, and terminal costs covers Shane's time) Restock and maintenance are under 2 hours/week per machine The operator relationship is durable (not at risk of being pushed out) At 2–3 machines, a simple route becomes possible: restock all machines in a single 3–4 hour loop per week. East Portland pod density makes this feasible — most target pods are within a 5-mile radius of each other. Beyond 3 machines, consider the "Rent-a-Human" ops layer from ../topics/hot-sauce-vending-machine.md — paid field execution for stocking and maintenance, freeing Shane to focus on product and terminal decisions rather than logistics.

text: Home Recipes This page captures simple repeatable recipes worth keeping in Shane's personal operator wiki. The point is not culinary completeness. It is to preserve low-friction, proven household recipes that are easy to remake without hunting through chat history. Quick Dutch Oven Bread A durable keeper recipe for a simple rustic loaf. Ingredients 3 cups white flour 1 cup whole wheat flour 2 1/4 tsp yeast 2 tsp salt 2 cups warm water Add 2 to 4 tbsp more flour if dough is too wet Directions Mix flour, yeast, and salt. Add warm water. Stir until shaggy and sticky. If it looks like batter, add 2 tbsp flour. Add a little more if needed. Cover and let rise 1 1/2 hours. Put Dutch oven with lid in oven. Uncover and bake 10 to 15 minutes more. Cool before slicing.
