text: Hot Sauce Vending Machine A vending machine stocked with a friend's artisan hot sauce, placed at food cart pods, accepting Bitcoin Lightning and credit card. Low overhead, no staffing, bitcoin-native POS, local product distribution. Why this matters now This is the first concrete "owned spend surface" for the local bitcoin-commerce lane. It does three jobs at once: creates a place where sats can actually be spent locally proves out the Lightning + card payment stack on real hardware gives Shane a physical product/business experiment that can expand into coffee, drinks, or other local goods later The Core Concept **Product**: Friend's hot sauce (consignment or wholesale split) **Placement**: Food cart pods — high foot traffic, food-curious audience, no direct competition with the carts **Payments**: Lightning Network (instant, ~1% fees) + credit card (Stripe Terminal or Square) **Ownership**: Shane owns and operates the machine; friend gets per-bottle revenue share Why Food Cart Pods Work Captive audience already in a "spend money on interesting food" mindset Pod operators often welcome complementary revenue — you're not competing with their carts Portland has dozens of pods with different vibes; easy to test 1-2 before scaling Low bureaucratic friction: placement on private property (pod owner permission only, no city permit needed for the machine itself) Hot sauce is an impulse buy at $8–$15/bottle — perfect vending price point Payment Stack Options Option A: BTCPay Server + Lightning (Bitcoin-first) Self-hosted BTCPay Server on a Raspberry Pi or VPS Lightning invoice QR shown on screen; payment confirmed in seconds Add Stripe Terminal (physical card reader) for credit card alongside it Fees: Lightning ~0–1%, Stripe ~2.7% + $0.05 Best for: bitcoin-native branding, no middleman, full control Reference: BTCPay Server POS — open source, free Option B: OpenNode or Strike (hosted Lightning) Managed Lightning without running your own node Easier setup, slightly higher fees (~1%), less control Good for MVP before committing to self-hosted stack Option C: Square + Cash App (easiest, least bitcoin) Square Terminal handles card + Cash App Pay (which supports Lightning via BOLT11) Fastest path to deployed hardware Tradeoff: no native Lightning wallet QR, Cash App intermediary Bolt Card (NFC Lightning tap-to-pay) Customers with a Bolt Card tap NFC to pay Lightning instantly No QR scan needed — slick UX, especially for regulars Worth supporting if going full bitcoin-native Settled recommendation After current-source review, the best first serious stack is: **BTCPay Server for Lightning** **Stripe Terminal for cards** **Qibixx MDB Pi Hat Plus or MDB-USB for vending control** Recommended card-reader choice: **Best unattended path**: Stripe Verifone UX700 if available, because Stripe positions it for self-service and recommends server-driven integration for it. **Fallback faster-to-start path**: a more attended tablet + reader setup before moving to a fully self-service reader enclosure. Why this wins over the earlier menu of options: It keeps Lightning on an open, self-hosted stack. It gives a realistic card path for normal customers instead of forcing Bitcoin-only behavior too early. It avoids writing raw MDB protocol from scratch because Qibixx now exposes a higher-level interface. It leaves room for future NFC/Bolt Card support without making that the Day 1 blocker. Hardware Options Off-the-Shelf Vending Machine Standard snack/small-item vending machine ($800–$3,000 used, $2,000–$5,000 new) Refrigerated not needed for shelf-stable hot sauce Bolt on a tablet (iPad or Android) running BTCPay POS app + Stripe Terminal reader Sources: eBay, Craigslist, vending machine liquidators Custom / Smaller Format Small countertop "smart locker" style (3–12 slots) — lower footprint, easier to negotiate placement Companies: Adimac, or DIY with Raspberry Pi + servo locks + touchscreen Better for testing before committing to full-size machine The "Dude, Seriously" Precedent Dude, Seriously already launched the world's first hot sauce vending machine at a food/drink venue in Cincinnati Proves the concept works and people engage with it Differentiation: go bitcoin-native + local craft product + food cart pod context Business Model | Revenue Source | Notes | |---|---| | Per-bottle margin | Buy from friend at wholesale (~$4–6), sell at $10–$14 | | OR consignment split | Friend gets 50–60%, you keep 40–50% per bottle | | Placement fee to pod | Typically $0 if you bring traffic; sometimes small monthly fee | | Bitcoin premium | Consider BTC-only price at $0.50 less — encourages Lightning adoption | *Unit economics example** (wholesale model, 20 bottles/week): Revenue: 20 × $12 = $240/week COGS: 20 × $5 = $100 Payment fees (~2%): ~$5 Gross: ~$135/week per machine (~$7k/year) Placement Strategy **Start with 1 pod** — negotiate a handshake deal with the pod operator (offer revenue share or flat $50–100/month) **Target vibe**: pods with a "foodie + adventurous" crowd, not just lunch workers **Portland pods worth approaching**: WonderLove PDX (SE Portland, elevated vibe), pods near Alberta Arts District, Mississippi Ave **Pitch to operator**: "I bring a unique attraction, zero staffing, and I handle restocking 1x/week" **Scale**: once one location is profitable and dialed in, clone to 2–3 more pods Field Ops / "Rent-a-Human" Even a low-staff machine still needs real-world operations. A lightweight human support layer can cover: weekly restocking jam checks and machine resets card reader / screen troubleshooting venue relationship maintenance in-person merchant discovery while already out servicing the machine That makes this lane a good fit for a "Rent-a-Human" style offer: paid field execution for local bitcoin-commerce infrastructure. Bitcoin Angle / Branding Ideas Machine wraps with "Pay with ⚡ Lightning" prominently — conversation starter First purchase free with Lightning (loss leader for onboarding) QR code on machine links to a simple "how to use Lightning" explainer Name the machine something fun — "The Sauce Stack", "Hot Node", "Capsaicin ATM" Partners naturally with CashForClankers bitcoin-curious audience MVP Build Path Source a used snack vending machine with MDB support Set up BTCPay Server store + PoS / API flow for Lightning invoices Use Stripe Terminal for card acceptance Add Qibixx MDB interface so successful payment can trigger vend approval Load with friend's hot sauce Negotiate placement at 1 food cart pod Run for 60 days and track sales mix: Lightning vs card, top SKUs, failure modes, service burden Decide whether to: keep scaling hot sauce add coffee / drinks or spawn a kid-friendly toy capsule variant For the concrete sub-work: hardware/vendor judgment lives in vending-terminal-buyers-guide.md comparable real-world builds live in btc-vending-machine-examples.md placement and host outreach lives in vending-machine-location-pitch.md Open Questions Does the friend want to be involved operationally, or pure product supply? Refrigerated or room-temp storage? (most craft hot sauces are shelf-stable) What's the restock cadence? (weekly is easy at food cart pod distance) Machine ownership: buy used vs lease vs build custom? title: Kids Sats Toy Vending
summary: The goal is simple: make sats feel real to kids by letting them share small balances and buy a toy, sticker, capsule, or reward from a machine.
text: Kids Sats Toy Vending The goal is simple: make sats feel real to kids by letting them share small balances and buy a toy, sticker, capsule, or reward from a machine. This is not mainly about profit. It is about: teaching what money does making Lightning feel concrete creating a family-friendly local Bitcoin ritual giving kids a reason to receive, save, share, and spend sats Settled recommendation The best first kids stack is: **LNbits** for isolated kid wallets and small-balance management **NFC cards** for easy tap-like spending **Bolt Cards later** for safer recurring use and a more polished tap-to-pay experience **A token-based toy capsule machine** for the first physical machine Why this stack wins: LNbits is explicitly designed as an account system sitting on top of a Lightning funding source. LNbits documents NFC spending via LNURLw on simple cards and recommends the Boltcard extension for bigger amounts. Bolt Card is purpose-built for merchant point-of-sale Lightning payments and supports per-transaction or per-day rules. Token-based toy machines are cheap, rugged, and already sold as rewards systems for kids, schools, and home use. This avoids over-engineering the first kids build around full MDB automation before the educational loop is proven. Recommended kid payment flow Phase 1: supervised Each kid gets a tiny LNbits wallet Parent loads sats in small amounts Kid scans a QR or taps an NFC card Payment is confirmed on a small POS screen Parent hands over a token or triggers the toy vend manually This is enough to teach: balance price paying choosing between spending now or saving Phase 2: token-backed machine Kid pays sats into a simple family POS POS earns or dispenses a .984 token Kid uses token in the capsule machine This is lower risk than direct machine automation and still feels magical. Phase 3: direct Lightning machine Replace token redemption with direct electronic vend control Add Bolt Card tap-to-pay for repeat use Add small screens or item labels priced in sats That is the stage where a smarter custom dispenser or MDB-connected toy machine starts making sense. Machine options Best first hardware: token-based capsule machine Current practical options: **CandyMachines Rhino Toy Capsule Rewards Machine**: positioned as a rewards machine for schools, pediatric offices, and home use, with a .984" token mechanism pre-installed. **Gumball.com Big Pro 25" Toy Machine**: all-metal 2-inch capsule machine with upgrade options for .984 token, 75¢, or $1 mechanisms. Why this class of machine is good: cheap compared with full snack vending durable and mechanically simple visually exciting for kids works with collectible toy capsules, stickers, squishies, or challenge cards Toy / reward ideas Good vending content should be cheap, safe, and collectible. Best first items 2-inch capsules with small squishies or fidget toys sticker capsules temporary tattoos tiny animal figures joke slips or scavenger-hunt challenges "mystery sats" cards with a QR for a tiny LNbits top-up Better than random junk If possible, make the rewards teach something: "save 3 buys and unlock a bigger item" "share 100 sats with your sibling and earn a bonus sticker" "scan this card to claim a mini allowance" collectible characters themed around sats, nodes, mining, lightning, or saving Wallet / NFC design LNbits layer Use LNbits because it is good for: tiny segregated balances family-safe experimentation not exposing a full main wallet to a toy machine setup NFC choice **Small balances**: simple NFC cards based on NTAG216 are enough for early experiments **Bigger recurring balances**: move to Bolt Cards The right mental model: NTAG216: cheap training wheels Bolt Card: polished reusable debit-card experience Teaching design The machine should teach one concept at a time. Ages roughly 4-7 "tap / scan and a toy comes out" learn that money is finite learn that prices differ Ages roughly 7-10 compare toy prices in sats choose between saving and spending send small amounts to siblings or friends Ages roughly 10+ understand that this is Bitcoin on Lightning learn custody vs app wallet vs card help run the family vending experiment Recommended build path Set up LNbits for a family-safe wallet layer Create tiny kid balances and simple QR/NFC payment objects Buy one token-based capsule machine Start with 2-inch toy capsules and a few educational reward inserts Price rewards at psychologically simple sats amounts Watch behavior: what do kids actually choose, save, or share? Only then decide whether to automate direct dispensing Pricing ideas low-value sticker / tattoo / joke capsule: 100-300 sats standard toy capsule: 300-800 sats premium capsule or mini challenge pack: 800-1500 sats The exact number matters less than making tradeoffs visible. Why this matters to the broader circular economy lane Adult commerce proves merchant viability. Kids commerce proves cultural adoption. If kids in a family or neighborhood learn: "I have sats" "I can send sats" "I can buy something real with sats" then the local Bitcoin economy stops being abstract adult tech talk and becomes normal social behavior. text: Lateral Bets — Hot Takes and Open Questions Most Shanepedia lanes are tracked separately: vending, Bitcoin, OpenCluck, OpenClaw, El Salvador, content. The interesting bets live in the crossovers — where two or more lanes collide in a non-obvious way. This page is the running list. Each entry: why it is interesting, the first proof step, the biggest risk. None of these are committed projects — the point is keeping the speculation legible so it can be picked up when a lane ships a milestone that makes a bet ready. Lightning egg vending machine *The bet:** A small refrigerated vending machine at the farmland roadside (or a cooperating local business) selling dozens of eggs from Shane's flock. Lightning + card. Restocked twice weekly from the coop. *Why interesting:** Tightest crossover available — ../entities/opencluck.md produces the inventory, hot-sauce-vending-machine.md provides the vending playbook, bitcoin-circular-economy-portland.md provides the Lightning side. Cleanest content artifact possible: "I sold an egg my chicken laid for sats." *First proof step:** A single cooler-with-padlock honor box at the farmland gate with a printed BTCPay invoice QR per dozen. No machine. Validate demand before spending on cold-vending hardware. *Biggest risk:** Oregon ODA cottage food and farm-direct sale rules. Honor-box version is fine; refrigerated vending crosses into more regulated territory. Verify before any machine deployment. Short YouTube series documenting the OpenCluck build *The bet:** A 6–10 episode series, 4–8 minutes each, documenting OpenCluck from BOM to first deployed unit. Released as the build happens, not after. *Why interesting:** The intersection of "ESP32 builds" + "backyard chickens" + "self-hosted IoT" is small but loyal and underserved — chicken content is suburban-cute, ESP32 content is generic-LED. Almost no competition at the cross-section. Also accelerates open-sourcing the firmware under ../entities/cash-for-clankers.md. *First proof step:** Record a single 5-minute episode 0 with the BOM on a table. Post it without optimizing. See what comments arrive. *Biggest risk:** Video production overhead. Shane's edge is text, not video. If episode 0 takes 20 hours, the series won't survive a busy week. The episode-0 test measures that overhead before committing. Agentic Yelp for Bitcoin merchants *The bet:** A site that takes BTCMap data as a base, layers agent-driven verification (calls/messages the merchant, asks "do you actually accept Lightning?", logs the answer), and surfaces a freshness score. Updated weekly. Portland-only first. *Why interesting:** BTCMap is great as a community map but everyone who uses it knows the data is stale. A verification layer is the single most useful upgrade. Perfect agent task: structured input, structured output, runs on a cron. Crosses the OpenClaw stack with the circular-economy research lane. *First proof step:** Manually verify the 30 BTCMap-listed Portland merchants this week. Publish a single page with the results. If the answer is "12 of 30 still really accept Bitcoin," that itself is a story worth shipping. *Biggest risk:** Merchants do not love being cold-called by an agent. The bet only works if the verification is polite and the published data doesn't embarrass merchants who have honestly stopped. Lightning-paid coop monitoring as a service *The bet:** Productize OpenCluck. Small farm gets a sealed sensor unit, plugs it in, gets Telegram alerts. Subscription paid monthly in Lightning. Hardware sold at cost; recurring revenue is the alert service plus historical dashboard. *Why interesting:** Millions of US households keep home flocks; almost none have monitoring. A $15/month Lightning-paid sensor service is differentiated on three axes (Bitcoin native, agent-aware, open-hardware) against zero real competition. Combines the OpenCluck hardware, Bitcoin payment, and agentic operator-service lanes. *First proof step:** Deploy two units to friends' coops free for 90 days. See if alerts catch meaningful events and whether they'd have paid. *Biggest risk:** Hardware-as-a-service is operationally heavy. Shipping, RMAs, batteries — the support tail can eat a one-person op. Only works if the unit is genuinely plug-and-walk-away. SOUL.md template marketplace for OpenClaw users *The bet:** A curated catalog of personality templates (SOUL.md / IDENTITY.md / USER.md) for personal AI agents. Free templates plus a few paid premium ones — "Founder operator," "Researcher," "Solo dev who lives in terminal." *Why interesting:** Personal agents are about to become normal, and almost nobody knows how to write a SOUL.md from scratch. Real arbitrage between people who have tuned this for a year (Shane is in that set) and people who just turned on Claude Code last week. Crosses agent-personality-design.md with agentic-business-studio.md and produces a public artifact that markets the rest of the studio. *First proof step:** Publish three templates as a single GitHub repo under Cash for Clankers — Shane's sanitized SOUL/IDENTITY/USER, a researcher variant, a solo-dev variant. One-page README. See if anyone forks. *Biggest risk:** Templates feel uncanny when the user's voice differs from the template's. The real product may be a *tutorial* on writing your own, with templates as worked examples — not a marketplace. Test framing before committing. Lightning-invoiced WhatsApp reply desk for Los Cobanos operators *The bet:** The Whale Window Reply Desk from agentic-business-studio.md, but invoiced and paid in sats weekly via Lightning. No fiat. Combines the El Salvador operator-service lane, the agent-replies lane, and the Bitcoin-payment lane in a country where Bitcoin is legal tender. *Why interesting:** El Salvador is the one country where invoicing in sats is not weird. Removes the international wire / PayPal friction that kills most cross-border B2B services in the region. Marketing artifact: "AI reply desk for El Salvador tourism operators, paid in Lightning" is a genuinely novel offer. *First proof step:** One pilot operator, one month, fixed sats price. Run the agent-assisted reply flow over WhatsApp Business, document the booking conversion delta, get paid. If it works, the case study is the marketing. *Biggest risk:** Bilingual quality. Bad Spanish replies damage a small operator's reputation fast. The agent needs testing against native Salvadoran Spanish (not generic LatAm), with a human review loop fast enough to catch errors before send. How to use this page Not a roadmap. The legible side of speculation that would otherwise live as one-off notes. When a bet's first proof step becomes cheap (a lane shipped, a tool got better, the calendar opened), pull it down and convert it to a real project page. When a bet stops being interesting, leave it here as a record of why it didn't survive. The point is the crossover muscle — noticing when two lanes collide.

title: LLM wiki pattern
summary: The LLM wiki pattern is the idea that an LLM should maintain a persistent markdown wiki as an intermediate compiled knowledge layer between raw source documents
text: LLM wiki pattern The LLM wiki pattern is the idea that an LLM should maintain a persistent markdown wiki as an intermediate compiled knowledge layer between raw source documents and future queries. Contrast with ordinary RAG In ordinary RAG, the model repeatedly rediscovers relevant context from source fragments at query time. In an LLM wiki, the synthesis is compiled forward over time. The model updates pages, cross-references, summaries, and contradictions as new material arrives. Structural layers raw immutable source documents an LLM-maintained markdown wiki an instruction file that teaches the LLM how to ingest, update, query, and lint the system Adapted for Shanepedia and Codex In this environment the pattern becomes: raw/ as the evidence layer wiki/ as compiled founder/operator memory Obsidian as the human IDE for browsing the graph Codex as the primary maintainer writing durable updates OpenClaw child lanes as feeder systems that should improve the parent wiki That means good answers should usually leave a file behind. The system should gain pages, links, maps, dashboards, and clarified contradictions, not just terminal output. Why the pattern is powerful knowledge compounds instead of resetting every query useful analysis can be written back as durable pages cross-links and contradictions can be maintained incrementally the human gets a browsable system instead of a pile of uploads Obsidian becomes a real IDE for thought instead of just a note browser Shanepedia implication Shanepedia should explicitly act like this pattern, not merely resemble it. That means every ingest, question, and synthesis should be treated as an opportunity to improve the compiled wiki itself. Codex implication Codex should behave less like an ephemeral assistant and more like a wiki maintainer: parent wiki first child lane second raw source only when the compiled layer is missing or needs verification durable markdown output by default for reusable insight index, lint, and navigation upkeep as part of the task, not optional polish Product implication This is also one of Shanepedia Studio's strongest possible offers: an agent-maintained founder wiki that compounds context over time and becomes a durable operating system for projects, relationships, travel, research, and decisions. Business seed: Founder Pi Briefcase A Raspberry Pi or local-docker founder console that turns the LLM wiki pattern into a daily control surface: latest notes, open decisions, relationship prompts, and one-tap capture. Fits Shane's taste for fast, intentional interfaces: instant-boot screen, clear hierarchy, low chrome, and obvious next actions instead of dashboard sprawl. Agents maintain the markdown wiki, compile daily briefs, surface contradictions, and keep the founder memory layer durable without making the buyer learn a new system. Best first buyers are fast-moving founders with scattered chats, screenshots, and experiments who need a calm command center more than another SaaS tool. Can start as a setup + upkeep service, then expand into reusable hardware images, templates, and agent workflows across the founder OS lane.

text: Mac Agent Dev Stack Shane built a dedicated macOS AI agent development machine from scratch in 2026 using a sequential 11-phase setup guide (~/setup-mac). The project represents a deliberate philosophy: a workstation configured specifically for agent-first computing, not general-purpose software development. Philosophy The setup prioritizes security, speed, and reproducibility over convenience. Each tool is chosen for a specific role and guarded with nono kernel-enforced sandboxing. Secrets never touch config files. Scripts are idempotent. The machine is intended to run AI agent workloads, research automation, and multi-process agent orchestration reliably. The guiding principle: a machine that can run multiple AI agents simultaneously, with bounded permissions and clean tool isolation, is a force multiplier for a solo founder. Core tools *Runtime managers:** bun — fast JavaScript/TypeScript runtime used for QMD (quick markdown) tooling and agent scripts uv — Python package and environment manager; replaces pip/virtualenv with faster resolution and lockfile-first reproducibility Rust — systems-level toolchain for CLI tools and native binaries in the stack *Shell and terminal:** starship — cross-shell prompt with contextual status (git, runtime versions, nono sandbox indicator) Modern CLI replacements for standard Unix tools (ripgrep, fd, bat, eza, etc.) *AI operations:** Claude Code — the primary AI agent runtime; runs in the macOS terminal with MCP server integrations OpenClaw — the gateway layer above Claude Code; routes models, manages skills, connects Telegram nono — kernel-enforced sandbox; applies filesystem and network boundaries to agent processes per profile *Secret management:** macOS Keychain is the authoritative secret store Secrets are injected at runtime via nono --secrets, not stored in environment files or config API keys in ~/.zshenv are for shell-level access where Keychain injection is unavailable Setup phases (overview) The setup-mac guide runs 11 sequential phases from a clean macOS install: Base system configuration and XCode tools Homebrew and core formula Shell environment (zsh, starship, dotfiles) Language runtimes (Bun, uv, Rust, Go) AI tooling (Claude Code, OpenClaw, nono) 5-11. Project-specific tooling, integrations, secrets, and verification Each phase is a documented script with command -v guards so it runs safely on a machine that is partially configured. nono sandboxing model nono is the security boundary for all agent work. Profiles define allowed paths, network permissions, and tool access. The $WORKDIR variable is resolved at runtime, so the same profile works across different workspace roots without modification. The sandbox means agents can read and write files within their project scope, make allowed network calls, and execute configured tools, without being able to read secrets, touch other user data, or break out into system-level access. This is meaningful for an operator running research agents and AI-assisted automation on real business data. Why this matters for Shanepedia The agent dev machine is what makes the Shanepedia research flywheel operational. Without a configured, sandboxed, always-ready environment, each agent session requires manual setup and carries elevated risk. With it, Shane can launch research loops, wiki maintenance cycles, Telegram-driven agent sessions, and Cron-triggered automation from a stable base. The setup-mac project is also documentation of a replicable stack, which fits the agentic-business-studio model: the machine configuration itself is a potential product or template for other founders who want an agent-first workstation.

title: OpenClaw AI Gateway
summary: OpenClaw is Shane's self-hosted AI gateway and agent orchestration system. It functions as the central routing layer between Claude Code, skill definitions, Tel
text: OpenClaw AI Gateway OpenClaw is Shane's self-hosted AI gateway and agent orchestration system. It functions as the central routing layer between Claude Code, skill definitions, Telegram, and downstream tools. Most of the ongoing Shanepedia research and agent work runs through or is configured within OpenClaw. What it is OpenClaw exposes a unified interface for AI operations: model routing, agent skill registration, channel connections (Telegram, Claude Code), and tool access control. The canonical config lives at ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json and governs authentication, model selection, active agents, enabled channels, and tool permissions. The system is not a SaaS platform. It runs locally on Shane's machine with kernel-enforced sandboxing via nono. Secrets are stored in the macOS Keychain and injected at runtime, not embedded in config. Key subsystems *Skills** are the primary unit of agentic work. They follow the Agent Skills open standard: a directory with a SKILL.md file containing YAML frontmatter and markdown instructions. OpenClaw registers skills by name from the frontmatter, not the directory name. The canonical shared copy for each skill lives in ~/setup-mac/.agents/skills/. The wiki skill used to maintain Shanepedia is one example. *Workspace** holds personality and context files used to anchor agent sessions. The files SOUL.md, USER.md, and IDENTITY.md live in ~/.openclaw/workspace/ and give fresh agents grounding about who Shane is and how he operates. *Projects** under ~/.openclaw/workspace/projects/ include the full Shanepedia repo and child lanes like ElSalKB. This directory is where agent-maintained wikis, knowledge bases, and research artifacts accumulate. *Telegram channel** connects inbound messages from Shane's phone directly to Claude Code sessions. An agent running in remote mode receives Telegram messages as structured channel input and replies via the Telegram bot API. This makes OpenClaw the communication interface for mobile-to-agent operation. *nono sandboxing** is the security boundary. It is a kernel-enforced sandbox that restricts filesystem access, network calls, and system operations per profile. Profiles use a $WORKDIR variable resolved at runtime. This means agents can run with real file access inside a bounded perimeter without relying on software-level permission prompts alone. Operating model Shane operates OpenClaw primarily from the macOS terminal, with Claude Code as the active agent runtime. Telegram acts as the out-of-band control channel when he is away from the keyboard. Skills extend what Claude Code can do without modifying the core runtime. The pattern is: OpenClaw routes, nono sandboxes, Claude Code reasons, skills specialize, Telegram connects. Role in Shanepedia The wiki skill is registered in OpenClaw as wiki (from its SKILL.md frontmatter) even though the directory is wiki-gen. This is the entry point for all /wiki ingest, /wiki absorb, and /wiki query operations against the Shanepedia corpus. The Shanepedia repo itself lives in the OpenClaw workspace and is the target of all agent-driven research and synthesis. From the agent's perspective, OpenClaw is infrastructure. From Shane's perspective, it is the operating layer that makes a single person capable of running multiple AI-assisted research and build loops simultaneously. Configuration authority Edits to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json are the canonical change to system behavior. Skills, model routing, channel access, and tool permissions all resolve through that file. The Claude Code settings at ~/.claude/ configure the Claude Code runtime itself but are separate from OpenClaw's gateway-level controls.

title: Oregon Food Cart Pods — Operator's Read
summary: A food cart pod is a private surface lot hosting 5–30 mobile food carts in a fixed configuration with shared seating and (often) a permanent bar or coffee shop
text: Oregon Food Cart Pods — Operator's Read A food cart pod is a private surface lot hosting 5–30 mobile food carts in a fixed configuration with shared seating and (often) a permanent bar or coffee shop on the edge. The format is unusually concentrated in Portland and the east metro. For an operator deploying vending, alternative payments, or any small commerce experiment, pods are the most permission-loose, foot-traffic-rich, low-rent retail surface in the region. How a pod works Two layers of operator: **Pod owner / lot operator.** Owns or leases the lot. Sets up pad sites, runs power and water, builds covered seating, handles city permits, collects rent from carts. **Cart owners.** Independent operators who own their cart, pay $700–1,400/month stall rent (depending on location and utilities), and run their own food business. Each cart is a fully independent business — own permits, own LLC, own POS. The pod is the landlord. This split is the key to flexibility: the pod operator is incentivized by occupancy and traffic, not by what each cart sells. They will say yes to almost any tenant or amenity that increases foot traffic without headaches. Customers wander, order from one or several carts, eat at shared seating. Pods that work have covered seating or an attached bar anchoring evening traffic. Pods that don't work are exposed asphalt — they die in October and don't recover until May. Historical context: pre-COVID boom, post-COVID consolidation Portland's pod culture peaked roughly 2014–2019, with 600+ carts across dozens of pods. COVID hit the format hard: the famous downtown Alder/10th lot was sold off and redeveloped, and weaker pods folded. The strongest pods (Hawthorne Asylum, Prost Marketplace, Cartlandia, Hinterland) absorbed both customers and operator talent. Post-2022 the format stabilized at a smaller, more curated footprint — destination pods with covered seating and an anchor bar, neighborhood pods serving a defined crowd, and a few specialty pods (Asian, Latin, vegan). Cart counts are down from peak but per-pod foot traffic at the survivors is healthier than during the bloated 2018 peak. The format is not dying — it is leaner. Pods worth knowing (Portland and east metro) Not exhaustive. These are pods that have shown durability and operator stability sufficient to be worth approaching for any kind of placement deal: **Hawthorne Asylum (SE Hawthorne / 11th)** — large, covered, evening-and-weekend strong, diverse cart roster. The flagship survivor. **Cartlandia (outer SE 82nd)** — large, attached bar, popular with the Springwater Corridor cycling crowd, more of a destination than a walk-by. **Prost Marketplace / Mississippi Marketplace (N Mississippi)** — tight, well-curated, steady neighborhood traffic, attached beer hall. **5th Quadrant Pod / various Mississippi/Alberta clusters** — smaller, neighborhood-scale, lower rent, friendlier to experimental tenants. **Hinterland (Hillsboro)** — west-side, family-friendly, larger lot, a good template for what a successful suburban pod looks like. **BG Food Cartel (Beaverton)** — large suburban pod, family-leaning, indoor seating in a converted building. **Gresham downtown carts (Powell area)** — not a true pod cluster; individual carts on commercial strips. Lower density, less foot traffic, but closer to home base for any Gresham-anchored ops. The east metro / Gresham gap is real. Gresham has not developed a true pod culture the way SE Portland has. For any deployment that requires pod-density foot traffic, the relevant zone is SE and inner-east Portland; Gresham is for the second machine, not the first. See gresham-vending-ops.md for the deployment-side analysis. Operator dynamics — how to actually get in The pod owner is the gatekeeper, not the cart owners. It is almost always one person, not a corporate property manager. What pod owners want: more foot traffic, reduced friction for existing customers, predictable revenue with low management overhead (flat monthly preferred over rev share), no permitting drama. What they do not care about: the specific tech (most don't know or care what Lightning is), whether your product is innovative, whether your offer is "exciting." The right pitch is: "I want to put X on your lot, you get $Y/month flat, I handle everything, here is what it looks like." Short. Concrete. Reversible. Most pod owners will say yes to a $50–150/month flat-fee proposal for a small footprint amenity if the operator seems competent and the install is clean. Why pods are unusually friendly to vending and Bitcoin The part that matters for the studio thesis. Pods have structural properties that make them better than almost any other retail surface for vending and alternative payment experiments: **Single decision-maker.** One operator, one phone number. A strip mall is a property management company; a grocery store is a regional buyer. Pods compress the sales cycle from months to a single conversation. **Customers expect non-standard payment.** Cart regulars have used Square, Venmo QR, cash-only carts, tip-jar tablets. A Lightning QR is one more variant, not a foreign object. **Foot traffic is food-curious by definition.** Anyone walking a pod is opting into novelty. More likely to try a $12 hot sauce from a vending machine than a Walmart shopper is. **Power and shelter are usually available.** Outdoor outlets, covered seating, security lighting — deployment cost drops sharply compared to a standalone outdoor location. **Rent is low and lease terms are short.** $50–150/month for a small vending footprint vs. $2,000+/month for the smallest storefront. Order-of-magnitude difference. **Operator solidarity with the cart class.** Pod owners are themselves small operators. They extend the "let's see what happens" benefit in a way a corporate landlord never would. For Bitcoin: the next twenty Lightning-accepting nodes in Portland are more likely to be cart-pod machines and individual carts than standalone restaurants like ../entities/isla-bella-portland.md. Barrier for a Lightning cart is one tablet and a BTCPay account; for a restaurant it is staff training, POS integration, and accounting. Pods are the right substrate. What to verify before any deployment City permitting status of the specific lot (some operate under temporary use permits that constrain new tenants) Multnomah County Environmental Health rules for food sold from a vending machine Pod owner's existing exclusivity arrangements (some pods have a beverage exclusive with an attached bar) Insurance requirements for placement on a third-party lot Power load — older pods can run close to capacity on summer evenings Not show-stoppers. The kind of thing that turns a yes into a no if discovered late. Bottom line The pod format is the most operator-friendly retail surface in the Portland metro. For any vending experiment, Bitcoin onboarding play, or low-footprint commerce idea, pods should be the first three locations on the list. The format won't last forever — Portland real estate pressure will keep eating lot inventory — but the next 3–5 years are the cheapest, fastest path to put a small commerce experiment in front of real foot traffic.

It is not just another stop. It represents the decision to accept more logistical complexity in exchange for a genuinely different marine experience. title: Vending Machine Location Pitch — Finding and Winning Placements
summary: Before you buy a machine, you need a location. Before you get a location, you need a pitch. This page covers how to find placement targets, what to say, what te
text: Vending Machine Location Pitch — Finding and Winning Placements Before you buy a machine, you need a location. Before you get a location, you need a pitch. This page covers how to find placement targets, what to say, what terms to propose, and the business structure behind the ask. The fundamental trade you're making You are offering a business owner: **A free amenity** for their customers or staff **Passive revenue** (commission on sales) with zero effort on their part **Zero cost** to them — you pay for the machine, stock it, and maintain it In exchange you get: Floor or wall space (typically 4–8 sq ft) Electricity (typically 100–200W, negligible cost) Access to their foot traffic This is a mutual benefit deal, not a sales pitch. Frame it that way. Who to target first Tier 1 — highest probability of yes These venues have foot traffic, a captive audience, and a decision-maker who is easy to reach: **Auto repair shops**: customers wait 30–90 minutes with nothing to do. Owner is usually on-site. **Laundromats**: same dynamic. Long dwell time, bored customers. **Hair and nail salons**: waiting area foot traffic, women-dominated clientele good for snack/drink machines. **Small gyms and martial arts studios**: members want post-workout snacks; owner wants a member perk. **Tattoo parlors**: long sessions, clients and friends waiting. Good cultural fit for a Bitcoin vending machine specifically. **Coffee shops and co-working spaces**: Bitcoin-friendly demographics, ideal for a hot sauce or novelty machine. **Cannabis dispensaries** (where legal): high dwell time, cash-heavy customers already comfortable with alternative payment. Tier 2 — medium probability Office buildings (facilities manager, not owner — harder to reach) Hotels (regional manager approval often needed) Apartment complexes (property management company) Schools and colleges (requires facilities or admin approval; longer cycle) Tier 3 — lowest probability for small operators National chains (corporate approval, vendor credentialing required) Hospitals (strict health code requirements) Government buildings (procurement process) *Start with Tier 1.** You can place three machines in auto repair shops while a single hotel approval is still in legal review. Research before you walk in Spend five minutes before approaching: **Know the owner's name** — Google, Yelp, LinkedIn, Facebook business page **Know foot traffic roughly** — busy street? parking lot full? note it **Know what they already have** — no machine = opportunity; bad machine = replacement opportunity **Know what would sell there** — snacks/drinks for a repair shop, healthy options for a gym, novelty/Bitcoin-themed for a tattoo parlor You are not pitching a generic vending machine. You are pitching *this machine, for these customers, at this location.* The in-person pitch (recommended) In-person is always better than phone or email. You are asking for space in someone's business — they want to evaluate you as a person, not just a proposal. *Timing**: Go mid-morning on a weekday (10am–noon). Avoid Monday mornings and Friday afternoons. *Dress**: Clean, not formal. Business casual or nice-casual. You are a small local operator, not a corporation. Authenticity matters more than a suit. Opening line > "Hi, I'm [name]. I run a small vending operation in [city/neighborhood]. I was in the area and noticed you don't have a vending machine — I'd love to talk to you for two minutes about whether it might make sense here." If they say they're busy: > "Totally understand. Can I leave you my card and come back at a better time?" Core pitch (two minutes) > "I place and maintain [type] vending machines at local businesses. The way it works: I buy the machine, I stock it, I handle any maintenance. You don't pay anything. In return, I'd like to use [X sq ft] of your floor space near [waiting area / entrance / breakroom]. > > On the money side: I'd offer you [10–15%] of monthly revenue as a commission, paid monthly. At a modest [X] sales per day, that's roughly [$Y] per month for you — just for having the machine there. And your customers get a convenient option they didn't have before. > > Would you be open to trying it for three months?" If they ask about Bitcoin For a Bitcoin Lightning vending machine, use this frame: > "The machine accepts both regular card payments and Bitcoin Lightning — it's a newer payment rail that's instant and has no chargebacks. I'm piloting this at a few locations. It's not a gimmick — it's just another way to pay, and customers who use it tend to be enthusiastic about it. It also makes for good word of mouth." Do not over-explain Bitcoin. If they're curious, answer questions. If they're skeptical, acknowledge it and fall back to "card payments are the primary method anyway." The phone pitch Use this only as a follow-up after failing to reach the owner in person, or for Tier 2 locations. > "Hi, may I speak with the owner or manager? > > [Pause] > > Hi [name], my name is [name] — I'm a local vending operator. I'll keep this short. I place vending machines at businesses like yours at no cost to you — I handle everything. In exchange I pay a small commission on sales. I was curious if you'd have two minutes to hear more, or I could send a quick email with the details." The email pitch For cold outreach or follow-up after a call: -- *Subject**: Free vending machine for [Business Name] — small commission offer Hi [Name], I'm [Name], a local vending operator based in [City]. I'm reaching out because I think [Business Name] could be a great fit for one of my machines. Here's the short version: I provide and maintain the vending machine at no cost to you I stock it with [snacks / drinks / novelty items] You earn [10–15%] of monthly sales as a commission — typically $[X]–[Y]/month for a location like yours 3-month trial with no long-term commitment required Your customers get a convenient option, you get passive income and an added amenity — no work on your end. I'd love to swing by and take a look at your space. Would [Day] or [Day] work for a 10-minute visit? Thanks, [Name] [Phone] [Website or Instagram if applicable] -- The commission and contract structure Typical commission rates | Location desirability | Commission to host | |---|---| | Low traffic, off-street | 5–10% | | Moderate traffic, walk-in | 10–15% | | High traffic, captive audience | 15–25% | *Start at 10% for most locations.** Go to 15% if they push back or the location is excellent. Going above 20% typically only makes sense for truly premium placement (busy airport lounge, large gym, etc.). Fixed rent vs. commission Some owners prefer a flat monthly fee over a percentage: Flat fee pros: predictable for them, simple accounting Flat fee cons: you absorb all downside risk if sales are low *Proposed flat fee ranges**: $25–75/month for most small locations. Negotiate based on estimated sales volume. The placement agreement (contract) Always use a written agreement, even for a friend. Key sections: **Parties**: operator name, location owner name, business address **Equipment description**: machine make/model, serial number **Placement location**: specific spot within the business **Term**: start date, initial term (suggest 6–12 months), auto-renewal clause **Termination**: 30-day written notice by either party **Commission**: percentage of gross sales, payment schedule (monthly), payment method **Operator responsibilities**: stocking, maintenance, repairs within X days of reported issue **Location owner responsibilities**: provide electricity, reasonable access, notify operator of issues **Liability**: operator carries general liability insurance; machine is operator's property **Disputes**: state/county jurisdiction for any disputes *Free contract templates**: VendSoft contract guide and GeniusVend template are good starting points. Insurance Before placing any machine, carry a **general liability policy** naming you as operator. Cost: $30–60/month for a small operator. Required by most serious locations. Provides protection if a machine malfunctions and causes injury or damage. The Bitcoin angle as a differentiator Most vending operators pitching the same location are offering the same commodity: snacks, Pepsi, cards-only. A Bitcoin Lightning vending machine is a differentiator. Use it selectively: **Tattoo parlors, crypto-adjacent businesses**: lead with it **Coffee shops, co-working spaces**: mention it as a feature **Auto shops, laundromats**: mention it only if they seem interested; card payments are primary **Conservative businesses (churches, schools)**: do not lead with Bitcoin; focus on card payments and reliability For Bitcoin-friendly locations in Portland, check BTCMap.org — businesses already accepting Bitcoin are pre-qualified and will understand the pitch immediately. Finding locations systematically Ground game (most effective) Walk or drive neighborhoods near your target area Note every laundromat, auto shop, gym, salon, tattoo parlor, coffee shop Build a spreadsheet: business name, address, owner name (if findable), existing machine (yes/no), visited (yes/no), outcome Aim to approach 20 locations for every 1 placement you close (industry average is ~5–10%, higher with Bitcoin differentiator and good pitch) Online research Google Maps: search "[location type] near [city]" — check street view for waiting areas Yelp: read reviews to understand the customer base LinkedIn: find the decision-maker at offices and gyms BTCMap.org: find Bitcoin-accepting businesses who are already warm to the idea Referrals After your first placement, ask the owner: "Do you know any other business owners in the area who might be interested?" A referral from a peer closes faster than any cold pitch. What the business model actually looks like Unit economics for one machine | Item | Estimate | |---|---| | Machine cost (used, good condition) | $800–2,000 | | Monthly stocking cost | $150–300 | | Monthly commission to location | $30–75 | | Monthly maintenance / electricity | $20–40 | | Monthly gross revenue | $400–800 | | **Monthly net (before machine payback)** | **$130–355** | | Machine payback period | 6–18 months | These are rough estimates. A great location (busy auto shop, gym with 200+ members) can hit $800–1,200/month gross. A poor location is $150–250. The 5-machine threshold Most vending operators say the business becomes meaningfully profitable at 5+ machines because: Fixed overhead (insurance, vehicle, tools) is spread across more revenue Route efficiency improves — you can service 5 machines in a half day instead of separate trips You have enough data to know which locations perform and which to exit Bitcoin Lightning upside If even 10–20% of transactions at a location go through Lightning: You have zero chargebacks (irreversible) You reduce card processing fees on that portion You own the sats — they can appreciate You become a node in the local circular economy The Lightning revenue is not the main business model. The main model is snack/product sales. Lightning is the differentiator that gets you placements and press. Next actions [ ] Walk 10 Tier 1 locations near your home or workspace and note which have no machine [ ] Build a simple spreadsheet: business name, type, owner name, date visited, outcome [ ] Draft a one-page PDF leave-behind (your name, what you offer, commission rate, phone/email) [ ] Get a general liability insurance quote (look at: Hiscox, Next Insurance, Insureon) [ ] Draft a placement agreement using the VendSoft template as a base [ ] Check BTCMap.org for Bitcoin-accepting businesses in Portland metro as warm targets References Legit Pitch Scripts for Vending Machine Locations (Food Truck Empire) How to Craft the Perfect Vending Machine Pitch (Vending Locator) 3-Step Sales Formula for Vending Machine Pitch (Vendpreneurs) Cold Call Script for Vending Machines 2025 (Callin.io) Profitable Vending Machine Locations Guide (VendSoft) Vending Machine Contract Guide (VendSoft) Vending Machine Location Agreements (DFY Vending) Revenue Sharing in Vending (DFY Vending) How to Get Vending Machine Contracts (Insureon) GeniusVend Contract Template BTCMap.org — find Bitcoin-accepting merchants

title: Vending Machine Terminal Technology — Lightning + Credit Card
summary: How to build or retrofit a vending machine to accept Bitcoin Lightning and credit card payments, display QR codes, and trigger dispensing on payment confirmatio
text: Vending Machine Terminal Technology How to build or retrofit a vending machine to accept Bitcoin Lightning and credit card payments, display QR codes, and trigger dispensing on payment confirmation. Recommended first stack The cleanest path is staged, not perfect on day one: Start with the easiest live checkout path: card payments plus a Bitcoin-friendly option that can ship fast. Add a Raspberry Pi / tablet layer that shows Lightning invoices and confirms payment. Integrate MDB only after checkout and venue placement are proven. For Shane's current lane, the right bias is "get one machine live" before optimizing for maximum sovereignty. Settled stack as of 2026-04-18 After current-source review, the recommendation is: Production recommendation **Lightning**: BTCPay Server **Card**: Stripe Terminal **Self-service reader**: Verifone UX700 if Stripe availability/cooperation is workable **Machine control**: Qibixx MDB Pi Hat Plus or MDB-USB **Host**: Raspberry Pi 5 or equivalent small Linux box Why: BTCPay already supports a web-based PoS app for brick-and-mortar usage and exposes a Greenfield API/webhook path for custom checkout logic. Stripe's UX700 is explicitly positioned for self-service use and Stripe recommends the server-driven integration for it. Stripe Terminal supports offline card storage for supported card payments when connectivity drops. Qibixx now exposes a high-level serial interface and separate VMC / peripheral capabilities on the Plus hardware, reducing custom MDB risk. Fast fallback if UX700 is too slow to obtain Keep **BTCPay Server** for Lightning Keep **Qibixx** for MDB Use a more attended card-reader flow first, then upgrade the card side later This preserves the core architecture while avoiding getting blocked on self-service reader procurement. The Core Architecture `` [Customer selects product] ↓ [Payment terminal shows QR code / tap NFC / card swipe] ↓ [Payment confirmed (Lightning instant / card ~2s)] ↓ [Raspberry Pi / ESP32 sends MDB dispense command] ↓ [Vending machine releases product] `` MDB Protocol — The Key to Vending Hardware *MDB (Multi-Drop Bus)** is the industry standard protocol for vending machine peripherals. Nearly all modern vending machines have an MDB port. To add a custom payment terminal: Your device presents itself as an MDB "cashless payment device" Customer pays via your terminal Your device tells the VMC (Vending Machine Controller) to vend VMC releases the product *MDB Adapters (plug-and-play)**: **Qibixx MDB-Pi** (~$150–200): Raspberry Pi hat that talks MDB. Easiest path. Qibixx.com **ESP32 MDB Cashless** (open source): nodestark/mdb-esp32-cashless on GitHub — DIY, cheaper **RS232-MDB converters**: rs232-mdb.com — bridges MDB to serial for any computer Payment Terminal Hardware Stack Option A: Raspberry Pi + BTCPay + Stripe Terminal (Recommended for MVP) *Components:** | Part | Cost | Purpose | |---|---|---| | Raspberry Pi 4 (2GB) | ~$45 | Main computer | | 7" touch display | ~$70 | QR code + UI | | Qibixx MDB adapter | ~$150 | Talks to vending machine | | Stripe Terminal M2 reader | ~$59 | Credit card swipe/tap | | Case + power supply | ~$30 | Enclosure | | **Total** | **~$354** | | *Software stack:** BTCPay Server (self-hosted on Pi or VPS) — generates Lightning invoices Custom web UI on Pi (runs locally, shows QR + payment status) Stripe Terminal SDK — handles card payments Python script bridges payment confirmation → MDB dispense command *Flow (Lightning):** Customer taps product on touchscreen Pi generates Lightning invoice via BTCPay API, displays QR Customer scans with Lightning wallet (Phoenix, Wallet of Satoshi, etc.) BTCPay webhook fires → Pi confirms payment → MDB dispense command sent Machine vends *Flow (Credit card):** Customer taps product Stripe Terminal prompts card tap/swipe Stripe confirms → Pi sends MDB dispense Option B: ESP32 + LNBits (Ultra-Cheap DIY) *Components (~$80 total):** ESP32 dev board (~$8) Small TFT display (~$15) MDB-ESP32 cashless firmware (GitHub) LNBits instance (free, self-hosted) for Lightning invoices No credit card support without adding a card reader, but suitable for a bitcoin-only machine. Option C: Tablet + Existing VMC Cashless Port Some newer vending machines have a built-in cashless device port (MDB ready). You can mount a tablet running: **BTCPay Server POS app** — generates Lightning QR **Square POS** — handles card, has Cash App (Lightning) integration **OpenNode terminal** — managed Lightning, simpler setup No hardware hacking required — just mount tablet and connect to MDB port. Reference Implementations (Open Source) Jellybean Vending Machine GitHub: elaineo/Jellybean Raspberry Pi + Lightning node + GPIO pin triggers Works without MDB — uses direct GPIO to control the vend mechanism Good starting point for custom-built smaller machines Ricardo Reis — Coke Machine + Lightning Hackster.io project Raspberry Pi 3 + 7" display + BTCPay Server + PUSHER for real-time payment notification PHP web server generates invoices, PUSHER webhook confirms, Pi triggers vend Complete writeup with wiring diagrams CryptoVend Tablet UI (Devpost) devpost.com/software/cryptovend-tablet-ui Tablet UI for Lightning vending machine — polished UX reference Payment-for-Vending-Machine (GitHub) iZnd/Payment-for-Vending-Machine QR code payment trigger system for existing machines NFC / Bolt Card Support Beyond QR codes, Bolt Card lets customers tap an NFC card to pay Lightning instantly — no phone needed, no QR scan. The card holds a Lightning address and deducts from it on tap. *Hardware needed**: NFC reader module (~$15, ACR122U or PN532) + Bolt Card NFC server This is the slickest UX for repeat customers — like an Orca card but for hot sauce. Connectivity Requirements The terminal needs internet to confirm Lightning payments (and card payments). Options: **WiFi** from the food cart pod (negotiate with operator — usually easy) **LTE hotspot** (reliable backup, ~$20/month) **Starlink** if you're ambitious and the pod is outdoors For Lightning: payment confirmation typically arrives in <2 seconds on a good connection. Build Priority for Hot Sauce Machine | Phase | What | Why | |---|---|---| | Phase 1 (MVP) | BTCPay + card checkout on an external UI | Validate pricing, placement, and payment demand | | Phase 2 | Add Qibixx MDB integration | Turn successful payment into real unattended vend control | | Phase 3 | Move to self-service card hardware such as UX700 | Cleaner production-grade kiosk flow | | Phase 4 | Add Bolt Card / NFC support | Best repeat-customer Lightning experience | Kids / family variant Do not force the adult vending stack onto the first kids experiment. For a kids sats-learning machine, the simpler recommendation is: **Wallet / accounts**: LNbits **Kid payment object**: NTAG216 NFC cards for tiny balances, later Bolt Cards for safer recurring use **Machine**: token-based toy capsule machine **Reason**: faster to deploy, lower breakage risk, easier to explain, still teaches "sats buy things" See kids-sats-toy-vending.md. References Qibixx MDB Adapter BTCPay Apps / PoS BTCPay Custom Integration Jellybean — GitHub Ricardo Reis Lightning Coke Machine — Hackster.io ESP32 MDB Cashless — GitHub BTCPay Server Bolt Card Stripe UX700 Reader Setup Stripe Offline Payments Square Cash App Pay MDB Protocol — Wikipedia

title: Vending Terminal Buyers Guide — Lightning QR Feasibility Matrix
summary: The core problem: most commercial vending terminals were built for Visa/MC/NFC. Lightning requires dynamic QR code generation tied to a live invoice. That is a
text: Vending Terminal Buyers Guide — Lightning QR Feasibility Matrix > Research confidence: mixed. Hardware specs are verified from vendor docs. Bitcoin/Lightning integration is partially confirmed — noted per row. The core problem: most commercial vending terminals were built for Visa/MC/NFC. Lightning requires dynamic QR code generation tied to a live invoice. That is a software integration problem, not a screen problem — but the screen still needs to be color and large enough to scan. This page answers: which terminals can physically display a Lightning QR, which have an API path to route payments through a crypto gateway, and what the realistic integration complexity is. Why Lightning QR is different from card payments Standard card terminal: Customer taps card → terminal talks to processor → processor approves → vend Lightning terminal: Customer selects product → terminal requests invoice from Lightning node/gateway → gateway returns a QR string → terminal renders QR on color screen → customer scans with phone → Lightning payment confirmed (< 2 seconds) → gateway webhooks the terminal → terminal triggers MDB vend command The difference: the terminal must be able to **request and render a dynamic QR on demand**, not just read a static payment token. This rules out older black-and-white or button-only readers. Terminal comparison matrix | Terminal | Screen | QR capable | API path | Crypto gateway path | Confidence | Source | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Nayax VPOS Touch** | 2.4" color touchscreen | Yes — native QR support documented | Cortina API (third-party gateway hook) | BitPay, OpenNode, GoCrypto via Cortina | Medium — API confirmed, crypto path theoretical | Nayax developer hub | | **Cantaloupe Engage Pulse** | Edge-to-edge color touchscreen | Yes — designed for dynamic QR | Cantaloupe SDK / Seed API | Bakkt partnership (bitcoin via Bakkt app); Lightning path unconfirmed | Low-Medium — Bakkt bitcoin path confirmed in 2021, Lightning unconfirmed | Cantaloupe store | | **Raspberry Pi + 7" touchscreen** | 7" color, full control | Yes — full custom | Any (BTCPay, LNbits, OpenNode) | BTCPay Server — fully verified | High — proven in DIY builds | Hackster.io Ricardo Reis build | | **ESP32 + TFT display** | Small TFT, low cost | Yes — custom firmware | LNbits LNURL API | LNbits — verified | High — open source build exists | GitHub mdb-esp32-cashless | | **CPI / Crane readers** | Varies by model | Depends on model | CPI SDK (enterprise) | No native crypto; custom middleware possible | Low — no public Lightning doc found | CPI developer docs | | **Ingenico / Worldline** | Color touchscreen (newer models) | Yes on newer models | REST API | No native crypto; middleware retrofit possible | Low — enterprise path only | Not publicly documented | | **Tablet (any Android/iPad)** | Large color — best for scanning | Yes — full control | BTCPay POS app, OpenNode app | Both fully verified | High — easiest QR UX, no MDB needed initially | BTCPay Server POS | What is actually confirmed by primary docs: Nayax officially documents Cortina DynamicQR, and its docs say the integrator returns QR data that is displayed on Nayax devices. Nayax officially positions VPOS Touch as supporting QR-based payments. BTCPay officially documents a public PoS app that runs on a web device for in-person checkout. What is still not confirmed: a public, production Lightning deployment on Nayax VPOS Touch a public, production Lightning deployment on Cantaloupe Engage Pulse any off-the-shelf Lightning plugin from Nayax or Cantaloupe Nayax VPOS Touch — detailed notes *What it is**: Nayax's flagship unattended payment device. Widely deployed globally. Accepts EMV, NFC (Apple/Google/Samsung Pay), QR codes (Alipay, WeChat Pay confirmed), and magnetic stripe. *Screen**: 2.4-inch color touchscreen. Small but functional for QR scanning. *The Cortina API** is Nayax's third-party gateway integration layer. It allows an external payment provider to act as the payment processor for the VPOS Touch. Flow: Machine sends payment request to Cortina endpoint Cortina routes to the configured gateway (normally a card processor) With modification: route to a crypto gateway (BitPay, OpenNode, GoCrypto) instead Gateway returns a QR string or payment URL VPOS Touch renders it *Confidence caveat**: Nayax's public docs confirm Cortina works for "loyalty cards, closed-loop payment methods, and custom payment flows." They do not explicitly name Bitcoin or Lightning in any developer docs found. The path is technically plausible but requires direct Nayax developer engagement to confirm. *Spark API**: A separate Nayax API for initiating sessions and handling card payment flows from a backend. Less relevant for Lightning but worth knowing exists for hybrid setups. *Recommended action**: Contact Nayax developer support and ask specifically: "Can the Cortina API be configured to route to a third-party Bitcoin Lightning gateway like OpenNode or BTCPay Server? Has anyone done this before?" Nayax developer hub: https://developerhub.nayax.com/ Cortina API reference: https://developerhub.nayax.com/reference/cortina-api-overview Cantaloupe Engage Pulse — detailed notes *What it is**: Cantaloupe's modern touchscreen card reader for vending and amusement. Replaced the E-Port G11 in Cantaloupe's lineup. *Screen**: Edge-to-edge color touchscreen. Larger and higher-res than the VPOS Touch. Better QR scanning UX. *Crypto history**: Cantaloupe announced a Bakkt partnership in 2021 allowing customers to spend bitcoin and supported loyalty points through the Bakkt app on Cantaloupe's unattended retail network. This was a custodial integration — customer pays through Bakkt, Bakkt settles through the Cantaloupe flow. Not a Lightning integration. *Lightning status**: No confirmed native Lightning support found. The Bakkt path could theoretically be extended, but Bakkt does not offer Lightning payments. *Custom QR path**: Cantaloupe's SDK allows custom payment flows. A custom QR invoice from BTCPay or OpenNode could theoretically display on the Engage Pulse screen via the SDK. Not confirmed in production. *Recommended action**: Contact Cantaloupe and ask about custom payment gateway integration via their SDK. Ask whether the Engage Pulse can display dynamic QR codes from a third-party payment provider. Cantaloupe store: https://store.cantaloupe.com/products/engage-pulse Cantaloupe card readers: https://www.cantaloupe.com/products/point-of-sale/card-readers/ Payment gateway comparison | Gateway | Lightning | On-chain | Self-custody | Fees | Best for | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | **BTCPay Server** | Yes | Yes | Yes — you control keys | 0% (self-hosted) | Sovereign operators, custom builds | | **OpenNode** | Yes | Yes | No — custodial | 1% | Fast setup, API-first, developer-friendly | | **BitPay** | Yes | Yes | No — custodial | 1% | Enterprise integrations, Nayax/Cantaloupe targeting | | **GoCrypto** | Yes | Yes | No — custodial | Varies | European market focus, retail POS | | **LNbits** | Yes (Lightning only) | No | Depends on funding source | 0% (self-hosted) | DIY/family builds, low-cost deployments | *Recommendation for first machine**: BTCPay Server if you want sovereignty and control. OpenNode if you want the fastest path to a working API integration without self-hosting a Lightning node. The practical MVP path (verified) This is the path with the most confirmed working implementations: `` Tablet (Android or iPad) ↓ BTCPay Server POS web app (self-hosted or BTCPay.net) ↓ Lightning invoice generated → QR displayed on tablet screen ↓ Customer scans with Phoenix / Wallet of Satoshi ↓ BTCPay webhook fires → payment confirmed ↓ Raspberry Pi receives signal → sends MDB command ↓ Vending machine vends ` Cost estimate for this stack: | Component | Est. cost | |---|---| | Android tablet (8") | $80–120 | | Raspberry Pi 5 | $60 | | Qibixx MDB Pi Hat | $150–200 | | BTCPay Server (self-hosted VPS) | $5–10/mo | | Stripe Terminal M2 (card fallback) | $59 | | Case, cables, power | $30 | | **Total hardware** | **~$380–470** | This builds on the Ricardo Reis Coke machine build and the CryptoVend Devpost project. Integration path decision tree ` Do you want commercial-grade hardware (Nayax/Cantaloupe)? YES → Contact Nayax/Cantaloupe dev support first to confirm Lightning gateway path If confirmed: use Cortina API (Nayax) or Cantaloupe SDK + OpenNode/BitPay If not confirmed: fall back to tablet overlay on existing machine NO → Use Raspberry Pi + tablet stack with BTCPay Lowest risk, most documented, full sovereignty `` Open questions (as of 2026-04-19) [ ] Has anyone confirmed a production Nayax VPOS Touch + Lightning payment in the wild? [ ] Does Nayax's Cortina API accept arbitrary third-party gateway URLs, or is the list of approved gateways fixed? [ ] Can Cantaloupe Engage Pulse display a custom BTCPay QR via their SDK without a Bakkt account? [ ] Does OpenNode have a pre-built Nayax Cortina integration available? These should be answered by direct vendor outreach before buying commercial hardware. The DIY Raspberry Pi path can start without any of these answers. text: WhatsApp booking funnels WhatsApp is the primary booking channel for small tourism operators in El Salvador. Most operators run their entire business through WhatsApp but have no structured funnel. This is a concrete, sellable service. Current operator pattern Tourist finds operator through word of mouth or a random Google listing Tourist sends WhatsApp message: "do you do tours?" Operator replies with price and availability (sometimes hours later) Back-and-forth about dates, group size, pickup location Booking confirmed via text, payment on arrival (cash or sometimes Bitcoin) Problems with this pattern No after-hours response — lost leads while operator sleeps No pre-built responses for common questions No photos, itineraries, or social proof in the chat flow No follow-up or review request after the experience No way to handle English-speaking tourists if operator speaks limited English No upsell or cross-sell of related experiences Better funnel design Stage 1: Landing page with WhatsApp CTA Simple single-page site with: hero photo, what you get, price, seasonal info, WhatsApp button Button pre-fills a message: "Hi, I'd like to book [experience] for [date]" Page loads in under 2 seconds, works on any phone Stage 2: WhatsApp Business quick replies Set up WhatsApp Business (free) with: Greeting message with key info Quick reply templates for pricing, availability, directions Photo catalog of experiences Bilingual responses (Spanish + English) Stage 3: Follow-up automation After experience: send thank-you + review request Before peak season: send reminder to past customers Use WhatsApp broadcast lists (not groups) for announcements Pricing this as a service **Basic site + WhatsApp setup**: $150-300 one-time **Monthly management** (respond to English leads, post updates): $50-100/mo **Full funnel build** (site + WhatsApp Business + templates + photo shoot): $500 First targets Victor at Los Cobanos (whale watching, reef snorkeling) Coffee finca operators on Ruta de las Flores Surf instructors at El Tunco and El Zonte Boutique hotel/hostel owners without proper booking flows Agent automation opportunity Agents can: Generate landing page copy from operator photos and descriptions Create bilingual WhatsApp quick-reply templates Monitor and flag unanswered WhatsApp leads Draft follow-up messages and seasonal announcements A/B test different CTA copy on landing pages Business seed: WhatsApp Season School A subscription for place-based guides and hosts that delivers monthly bilingual WhatsApp reply packs, seasonal promos, and one simple landing-page update. Best first users are Victor at Los Cobanos, coffee finca operators on Ruta de las Flores, and surf instructors with inconsistent English follow-up. Agents can turn operator photos, pricing notes, and seasonality into ready-to-send replies, CTA copy, and reminder broadcasts. Price could start around $59 to $149 per month, positioned as "more bookings without learning new software." Proof comes from a first cohort with one marine operator and one finca operator, measured by faster replies and more completed bookings. Business seed: Referral QR Table Cards Sell coastal hotels, cafes, and surf hostels a small printed table-card or lobby placard with a QR code that opens a prefilled WhatsApp booking chat for a trusted operator. Best first pair is Victor in Los Cobanos plus one nearby hotel or restaurant that already gets tourist questions but does not monetize referrals. The deliverable combines a micro landing page, a prefilled WhatsApp CTA, and a lightweight referral tracking sheet so partners can see which placements generate bookings. Agents handle bilingual copy, QR destination setup, partner-specific variants, and weekly message/reply refinements without adding software complexity for operators. Price it as a fast-launch referral funnel, with setup plus monthly optimization for seasonal offers like whale watching, snorkeling, or weekend packages.

text: YouTube randomness to Shanepedia spark YouTube randomness can be useful if it is treated as a playful discovery input, not as a feed to be obeyed. The idea is to let one odd, interesting, or surprisingly practical video become a tiny Shanepedia maintenance prompt: does this connect to an existing page, deserve a new note, or get ignored? Shape of the loop Pick one public-safe YouTube find from a random-interesting source, subscribed channel, search rabbit hole, or manual share. Extract only the useful signal: the concept, operator pattern, product angle, visual reference, or question it raises. Match it against Shanepedia pages before creating anything new. Turn it into one compact spark candidate for the daily loop. If it earns a yes, update the relevant page with a small durable note and source link. Good inputs a strange vending format that could inform hot-sauce-vending-machine.md, bitcoin-toy-store.md, or gresham-vending-ops.md a local-business marketing teardown that improves micro-site-factory.md or whatsapp-booking-funnels.md a founder workflow or agent demo that belongs near llm-wiki-pattern.md or agentic-business-studio.md a travel/operator video that changes how an El Salvador or Portland page should be framed a design, interface, or storefront pattern that is memorable enough to reuse Output contract The useful artifact is not a video summary. It is a Shanepedia spark: > YouTube spark: [specific public video idea]. It might connect to [existing page] because [practical reason]. Add a note, update the page, or ignore it? The message should stay small enough for Telegram and should not include private viewing history, account data, cookies, recommendations, or anything that depends on a logged-in feed. Why it fits Shanepedia Shanepedia already wants ideas to compound through the ../ops/shanepedia-research-flywheel.md and the ../ops/daily-random-spark-loop.md. YouTube randomness adds a more playful input lane: less formal than research, but still useful when the best bits are routed into the wiki instead of becoming another lost browser tab. The quality bar is simple: the video has to improve a page, sharpen a product idea, or create a better question. If it only feels entertaining, it can stay entertainment. Cron behavior The daily spark cron may ask Gemini for one public YouTube-flavored idea, but Gemini is optional. If Gemini is at capacity, unauthenticated, or slow, the job should fall back to wiki-native candidates and still send a useful text. Randomness should add taste, not fragility.
